author: Soreti Kadir
title: The city beneath the capital
content:
At the end of 2010, I took a trip to Ethiopia to visit my family. At the time, my parents worked in Bole, the commercial center of Addis Ababa. As I was only 16, my movements were more or less regulated by my parents, which meant that I would travel with them into the city each day, after which it was the extent of my curiosity and creativity (and pocket money) that determined what I did until evening, when I would head back to our house on the outskirts of the city. Slowly, interactions with the staff at a nearby cafe, just a few hundred meters from the building where my family worked, became routine.

Over the two months that I was in Ethiopia, with much of this time spent in Addis Ababa, we spent most of our lunch breaks together, hanging out on the steps of the cafe, sharing stories to pass the time. One day, the conversation turned to our relationship to “Ethiopia” as a national identity. I was raised in the Oromo diaspora, a community that, in the years my mother and I migrated to Australia, was made up mostly of political refugees who fled the country after the adoption of the 

Transitional Period Charter of Ethiopia

 and the official establishment of a transitional government.

This eventually led to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front monopolizing power within the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a process that resulted in the isolation of those seeking political power within the EPRDF through the ballot. Given the size and economic importance of the Oromia region, it was the Oromo Liberation Front, among others, that became a key target of political violence, creating political communities in exile exactly like the one that I grew up in.

I inherited a different definition of Ethiopia, colored by memories and experiences of violence and displacement that informed my relationship to the state as a place of unbelonging for those who shared my identity. The day that the conversation with these two new friends wandered into political territory, we all engaged passionately, striving to reflect the extent of both our personal experiences and hopes for our country. They found my reflections overly nostalgic, antagonistic toward the country’s future, and unconcerned with its good. I found their insistence that we shared a national identity inaccurate and offensive. We agreed on little, and I found it exhilarating.

That evening, I was restlessly anticipating the opportunity to tell my mother about what I thought was the most exciting experience of my trip to date. In recounting the story, I almost gave my mother a heart attack. Angry, afraid, and in shock, my mother warned me sternly against ever engaging in such conversation in public again. She asked me many questions about who these men were, how I knew them, and if we’d ever had such conversations before. What I was blind to, and what was the daily lived experience of my parents, was that Addis Ababa, primarily but not exclusively, was a heavily surveilled city, the state looking for the people doing exactly what I found myself doing that day — discussing the political reality of our country.

Thereafter, I was careful, out of curiosity more than fear (being 16 with a high risk tolerance will do that), and refrained from full-fledged conversations, opting for quiet inquiry when the opportunity presented itself. Although our conversation never veered down the road of politics again, I continued to visit my friends every day and remember rushing to say a heartfelt goodbye on the day I was due to fly back to Australia.

Other parts of the country carry their own nuances and political realities, which deserve their own analysis; my focus here is the capital, Addis Ababa. That afternoon at the cafe points to something larger: in Ethiopia, to nurture spaces of connection, community-building, and care, we must first invest in collective repair — of the damage wrought by decades of state surveillance, which has defined the range and breadth of relational life the city can hold, and of the legacy of what can only be described as settler colonialism. “Where,” figuratively and literally, can this process of repair take place? It must take place in Finfinnee, geographically the same location as Addis Ababa, but sociologically and historically different, and with a capacity unique unto itself to ground and lead us to new political possibilities.

In 1886, Menelik II conquered the lands that were then known as Finfinnee and were primarily inhabited by the Tulama Oromo. As it took on its new identity as the “new flower” (the meaning of Addis Ababa), as both a military barracks for the expansion of Menelik’s empire and as the accumulation point for capital extracted throughout the process of the Ethiopian state’s consolidation, Finfinnee lost something, an essence. Regaining connection with it, not just for the Oromo, but for all who inhabit the Ethiopian state, is vital if we are to become free of cyclical violence, political domination, and mass poverty. What matters here are the functions that Finfinnee held space for, which were specific to the Oromo’s indigenous ways of organizing society and were destroyed to make room for the functions of the modern nation-state’s capital city.

Historically, Finfinnee was the convergence point for the five 

Gadaa

 assemblies, representing the center of the loose confederation of diverse Oromo clan groups. This site of togetherness was activated not only for lengthy discussion and dialogue — unrestrained by time and space, taking months if needed, and sheltered only by the branches of the sycamore tree (known as the 

Odaa

) under which the meetings took place — but also as a place for collective connection with the natural world and the Creator.

Every year, the Oromo would converge in the millions to express gratitude for the change of seasons, for livelihood, and for collective life. This celebration, 

Irreechaa

, was banned under EPRDF rule, and although it was 

brought back

 by the current ruling party, what we now have is a pacified, desecrated, and heavily militarized version of the rite. This is because it was brought back to 

Addis Ababa

, not to 

Finfinnee

. If the return of 

Irreechaa

 had been to Finfinnee, rather than being performed as a plasticized event that seems to exacerbate ethnic animosities each year, it would serve as the site of dialogue and togetherness that it is meant to be.

In Finfinnee, the idea of a neighbor going without while your home is full is difficult to embrace. In Addis Ababa, your conditions and survival depend on whether or not you can successfully sell your labor. In Finfinnee, the idea of war as a solution, before all means of peaceful reconciliation are tried, even if these discussions take many months, would be an affront to what it means to inhabit the land. In Addis Ababa, war is a means to consolidate power and make those in the business of war richer. Finfinnee is governed by an entirely different set of ideals from those of Addis Ababa, and this suggestion that we find our way back to these ideals is neither archaic idealization nor the fruit of exclusionary nationalism with which many associate any discussion of Finfinnee versus Addis Ababa. Rather, for the city to make way for healthy public life to emerge, it has to lose its grip on its identity as a center of surveillance and as a place that offers itself as dignifiably livable for only the political and economic elite.

The song “Abba Bootii” (father of the gumboots), by Jaalee Amantee, uses both its lyrics and its music video to make intriguing and poignant commentary on the social and economic reality of this question of Addis Ababa versus Finfinnee. The gumboots, worn traditionally by male farmers and usually accompanied by a dress shirt, pants, a jacket, a woolen vest, a baseball cap, and a traditional white cotton blanket draped across the top half of the body, are an aesthetic commonly associated with farming communities on the outskirts of Finfinnee, the traditional lands of the Tulama Oromo. In the chorus, the singer tells his listener that he has endured enough of the contempt his own country shows him, and urges him onward to Finfinnee.

In the music video, we see a man intended to represent the Oromo who have embraced the aesthetics of modernity, stepping out of a car, dressed in semi-casual clothes. He sees mannequins dressed in the 

Abba Bootii

 aesthetic and proceeds to go and take selfies with them. As the chorus begins, the mannequins come to life and use their 

shimala

 — long sticks commonly associated with both farming and self-defense practices among the Tulama Oromo — to chase the man through the city, where he tries to escape by hiding behind different people, each of whom transforms into the 

Abba Bootii

, played by Jaalee himself. Eventually, the man ends up on land being plowed by a man (also Jaalee) with an ox, where he faces off with the mannequins, the cityscape visible in the background. We can interpret the act of taking a selfie with the mannequins, who also wear black masks to further symbolize erasure, and the ensuing confrontation as Jaalee’s attempt to return agency to the wearer of the gumboots in an Addis Ababa social and political environment where the way of life of those who work the land is subject to objectification and erasure.

Although this song is specific to the story of the northern Oromo farmers’ relationship to Addis Ababa and their relationship to the “modern” Oromo, its message reaches further. Acceptance and inclusion within the realm of Addis Ababa is conditional upon one’s ability to perform modernity, and this is not just limited to what one wears, but also includes what one thinks about the state project. What this song implies is that the aesthetic one chooses to adopt in Addis Ababa indicates to the surveillance systems how close or how far one may be from complying with the logics of capital and the state. It is not only the Oromo who would be subjected to this assessment in Addis Ababa; rather, any person representative of the majority subsistence farming class of Ethiopia would be eyed with caution in Addis Ababa, for their rejection of Addis Ababa would be a threat that, if it grew, could collapse the state entirely.

If Addis Ababa must fence itself off from the historic and contemporary realities that created and sustain it to safeguard its survival, then it must remain perpetually alert to any signs of the return to Finfinnee, which is as much a place as it is a political reality and mindset. Finfinnee is the site within Ethiopia where a multinational class revolution becomes a possibility. It provides the depth of recalibration needed for us to re-enter the communion of person-to-person dialogue, to extend mutual care and solidarity, and to remember a relationship to land that goes beyond extraction. Finfinnee 

is

 the third space.

author: Keston K. Perry
title: The imperialism of progressive economics
content:
Progressive economics has an imperial problem. It is possible to denounce inequality, defend redistribution, and criticize neoliberalism while preserving a deeper hierarchy: the presumption that experts, often based in powerful institutions in the Global North, can determine what justice should mean for societies shaped by slavery, colonial extraction, and imperial rule. The issue is not simply whether their intentions are good or their proposals sufficiently radical. It is who has the power to define the problem, decide which histories count and prescribe solutions after short field visits or, worse, on conference calls, before those most affected have determined the terms of repair.

This contradiction is particularly visible in debates about reparations and climate finance. Universal basic income, public ownership, cheaper credit, and expanded development finance can all be useful demands. None, however, returns stolen land, reverses accumulated colonial wealth, repairs ecological destruction, or restores collective authority over political and economic life. Redistribution and reparations can reinforce one another; they are not interchangeable. When the former is offered as a substitute for the latter, progressive universalism becomes a way of setting aside historically specific claims.

I encountered this argument during a debate about reparations in 2020. A senior economist asked where reparative claims should begin and end, questioned the feasibility of identifying descendants of enslaved people, and suggested universal income or shared dividends funded by wealth taxes as more practicable responses. The framing exposes an asymmetry: Why must restitution meet an exceptional test of feasibility while universal redistribution is treated as a reasonable starting point? Who decides which demands are too complicated to count as politics?

The point is not to dismiss universal social provision. It is to insist that the injuries of empire cannot be reduced to unequal household incomes. Colonialism reorganized property, labor, public finance, land tenure, and the authority to govern. Repair must be capable of transforming those relationships, not merely compensating people for living within them.

At a conference on African economic sovereignty in Dakar in 2022, I heard related arguments from progressive economists who treated nationalization or the green developmental state as ready-made alternatives to reparations. State ownership and planning can be indispensable instruments of transformation. Yet our meeting in the Museum of Black Civilizations was a striking setting in which to overlook the intellectual traditions and struggles through which African peoples have articulated their own visions of sovereignty. A model developed in one context does not become universal because its advocates consider themselves anti-neoliberal. The question is who defines the political horizon, and whose knowledge is allowed to unsettle it.

A similar dilemma runs through the international sustainability industry. Island and African societies confronting climate disasters are surrounded by consultants, conveners, investment platforms, and intermediaries promising innovation. International collaboration is not inherently objectionable. What matters is who controls the agenda, data, networks, and resulting resources. When communities supply experiences while outsiders translate them into fundable or bankable projects, an old division of labor survives under the language of partnership.

The Bridgetown Initiative brings these contradictions into focus. Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley has rightly drawn attention to the global financial system’s unequal treatment of climate-vulnerable countries. The initiative has pushed sovereign debt, liquidity, Special Drawing Rights, and multilateral development bank reform onto an international agenda that too often marginalizes small states. Yet recognition of an unjust financial architecture is not the same as transforming the relations of ownership and creditor power that sustain it. Expanded access to finance can leave the underlying distribution of wealth, risk, and power largely intact.

Consider what financial innovation means when disaster strikes. After Hurricane Beryl in 2024, Grenada activated a disaster clause that deferred debt-service payments. This created fiscal breathing room, but deferred payments were added to principal: relief in the timing of repayment, not cancellation of the obligation. Jamaica, meanwhile, received no payout from its catastrophe bond after Beryl because the contractual trigger was not met. Severe damage and financial eligibility are not the same thing.

Jamaica’s catastrophe bond subsequently paid out following Hurricane Melissa in 2025. That matters, and it would be misleading to suggest that these instruments never deliver resources. But the contrast between the two hurricanes sharpens the political question: Why is access to relief determined by predefined contractual thresholds rather than by the full extent of social need? A payout can be useful while the design of the instrument, its cost, its exclusions, and its distributional consequences remain open to criticism. Financial triggers are political choices, not laws of nature.

More fundamentally, why should societies that contributed so little to the climate crisis have to purchase protection against its consequences or assume further obligations to reconstruct after catastrophe? Debt pauses, contingent insurance, and additional lending may help manage immediate liquidity. They do not, on their own, undo the colonial and postcolonial processes that made public budgets fragile, infrastructure unequal, and coastlines vulnerable to extraction. An architecture organized around the next emergency risks treating the repeated production of vulnerability as a technical problem rather than a political relationship to be dismantled.

The critique cannot stop at international creditors. Caribbean leaders may invoke reparations on global stages while failing to confront land dispossession, concentrated ownership, and the exclusion of communities from decisions at home. Demands for justice from former colonial powers are legitimate and overdue. They do not exempt postcolonial governments from accountability for their own alliances with developers, financiers, and extractive industries. More money passing through the same structures of power does not necessarily produce more justice.

These questions connect Caribbean debates to African struggles over debt and restitution. The African Union made reparations for Africans and people of African descent a central theme in 2025. That agenda intersects with disputes over sovereign debt, resource extraction, the cost of capital, and the terms on which African states enter international markets. Across both regions, the question is not merely whether creditors can become more generous. It is how histories of colonial accumulation shaped the present distribution of wealth and risk — and who now possesses the power to change it.

There is also a tension between the reparative language of some political leaders and the demands of people confronting dispossession from below. Colonial rule organized economies around the extraction of labor and resources; independence did not automatically end that organization. Where postcolonial elites renew extraction through new partnerships and instruments, repair cannot be reduced to negotiating better terms for the same arrangements. It must ask who owns land and infrastructure, who defines value, who sets eligibility rules, and who decides what development is for.

What, then, would a different internationalism require? The Caribbean political economist Norman Girvan offered the language of “universality in diversity.” This is not an argument against shared emancipatory commitments. It is a refusal of the notion that every society must follow a single model formulated in a privileged intellectual center. A defensible universalism must emerge through exchange among different histories and political traditions, not through the export of supposedly complete solutions.

In practice, this means recognizing land defenders, workers, farmers, pastoralists, fisherfolk, Indigenous authorities, disenfranchised young people, and community organizers as producers of economic and political thought — not merely witnesses whose testimony experts interpret. It means communities exercising real authority over research agendas, ecological knowledge, budgets and the decisions that affect their land and livelihoods. Participation without the power to refuse, revise, or redirect a project is not self-determination.

It also requires changing the instruments and institutions of repair. Instead of asking only how to mobilize private capital, governments and international bodies should confront debt cancellation, grants rather than loans, land restitution and protection, public control of essential infrastructure, and community authority over reconstruction. Resources should sustain locally governed institutions and long-term ecological stewardship rather than subsidize projects designed elsewhere for private returns. These are not merely alternative funding mechanisms; they are different arrangements of power.

None of this romanticizes “the local” or assumes communities speak with one voice. Class, gender, race, indigeneity, and conflicts over land shape local politics too. Nor does it exclude economists, scientists, or lawyers from meaningful collaboration. Their expertise can be valuable when it is situated, contestable, and accountable to collective decision-making, rather than elevated above it.

The sequence must change. Instead of beginning with a universal instrument and asking communities to demonstrate their eligibility, begin with the histories, demands, and governing capacities of those confronting ecological and economic crises. Ask what they seek to repair, which institutions obstruct that repair and what material resources would enable them to exercise power. Only then ask which economic tools might serve those ends.

The imperial privilege of progressive economics lies in the authority to parachute in “feasible” solutions while treating the people whose lives are at stake as an afterthought. Good intentions cannot redeem that hierarchy. Repair demands more than a new vocabulary for development or more humane management of debt. It requires transforming the structures of ownership and knowledge that allow some to prescribe the future while others are expected to live with the consequences. The responsibility is not simply to listen, but to return power — and to change the conditions under which decisions are made.

author: Rose Nneoma Abba
title: Labors of liberation
content:
Ricci Shryock’s 

The Moon Will Not Burn Us

 is marketed as an account of the women who helped win the 11-year guerrilla war for independence from Portuguese colonial rule in Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde. Shryock’s book delivers on that promise with hyperrealistic scenes that drop you into mangrove forests where female teenagers and young adults shoot and dodge bullets, manage makeshift clinics, become mothers, devise new cooking technology, teach, gossip, and boil water for breakfast. 

It also exposes prejudice that women in the struggle faced at the hands of their fellow African men. A funny scene in the book exemplifies both the prejudice and the women’s handling of it. Shortly after Joana Gomes, a nurse and the book’s protagonist, joins a new base, the commander, who is also her distant cousin, threatens her that if she gets hurt, he will have to kill her. She replies that “as a nurse. . . .  even you, if you are injured and no-one can carry you I can give this medicine to you [to kill you].” As Carmen Pereira, a prominent guerrilla fighter with the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), nurse, and later acting head of state, famously observed: “In Guinea-Bissau, we say that women must fight against two colonialisms. One against the Portuguese, the other against men.”

But beyond illustrating women’s agency in the struggle, the book also offers timely provocations on our relationship with nature, the labor that sustains revolutions, elite-led movements, and the individual costs of collective struggle.

One of the book’s greatest strengths is its exploration of how the PAIGC’s vision of a future state manifested in practice long before victory was formally declared. The PAIGC was founded in 1956 to achieve independence for Guinea and Cape Verde from Portuguese colonial rule. For the party, building for the future state was just as vital as tearing down Portuguese colonial rule. 

This state-building effort is most visible in the book’s heartwarming scenes of education. We witness it when Joana’s father goes out of his way to secure teachers for his daughters. And again when 11-year-old Joana and her friends are instructed by Amílcar Cabral to teach the other teenagers on a boat trip from Guinea-Bissau to Guinea-Conakry. We learn that the PAIGC built 156 primary schools during the war across liberated territories compared to 11 created under Portuguese neglect. We also see the PAIGC send young Guineans to the Soviet Union and Cuba to master guerrilla combat tactics as well as medicine, engineering, agronomy, and teaching for the nation they were bringing into existence.

The book takes a firm stand: The success of a liberation struggle depends on the viable, egalitarian alternative structure you build to ground your sovereignty while you fight the oppressive power. As Shryock writes in the introduction, it is “a story worth knowing as a universal lesson in the undeniable courage it takes to imagine a new world, the way creation rather than destruction is integral to that new world.” Through Joana’s story, Shryock holds a steady lens on women’s central role in designing and executing that vital labor of building Guinean sovereignty from the ground up.

Shryock opens the book with a scene that haunts the entire reading experience: 22-year-old Joana inside a dry-season mangrove forest, where she had gone to retrieve a commander who was recovering from a lung infection. “Gnarly, bare mangrove branches protruding from the muddy riverbed stare back at [Joana],” setting the tone for the book from the very first page. 

The land, its trees, and its waters are alive. At times angry, at times hungry, mostly gracious, and systematically exploited by the Portuguese regime. And it was precisely this ecological exploitation that precipitated the revolution. Cabral, the founder of the PAIGC, was an agronomist by training, and his radicalization took root while he was conducting an agricultural census commissioned by the United Nations and the colonial Portuguese government. There, he saw firsthand how Portuguese land policies and price controls were squeezing the life out of both the land and the people tilling it.

As the Guineans fought for the land, the land protected them. Whether it is Joana tripping over an exposed root and narrowly dodging a bullet or people abandoning their towns to seek shelter in the forest, “besides the Soviets and the Cubans, the land [proved] to be the liberation fighters’ best ally,” Shryock writes.

Shryock’s writing of the gritty realities of the fighters’ encounter with nature serves as a necessary reminder that human survival ultimately rests on a nurturing and reciprocal relationship with the land. And by foregrounding and animating the landscape, the book invites an ecofeminist reading that exposes how colonial extraction of the land and gendered oppression draw from the same logic of subjugation that treats both the earth and women’s labor as infinite, free resources to be exploited without consequence.

It is understandable to witness a guerrilla war and assume the war began as a grassroots uprising. Shryock’s narration contributes to this illusion when she writes that “so, too, did the armed struggle not start in the capital. . . .  but deep in the countryside. . . .  in a rural and relatively isolated area,” referring to the first battle of the war in January 1963. Meanwhile, the party that led and coordinated the war’s efforts, including this battle, was founded in 1956 by urban Cape Verdeans.

History teaches us that even when elites carry the flag of revolution, popular discontent has usually fermented long before elite leadership articulates it. So it was with the PAIGC: They did not invent anticolonial anger, but they used their privileges to initiate and organize the revolution. The book shows the immense labor it took for urban, landowning, or comparatively privileged 

assimilado

 figures like Cabral and Joana to spread their vision of freedom, convincing rural people why their anticolonial rebellion mattered, why it could succeed, and why they should risk their lives for it. And as the war unfolds, readers experience the claustrophobia of the central command. We see Joana suddenly run into her cousins, siblings, or childhood neighbors leading command bases or brought to her care as wounded soldiers.

The story is marked by internal rivalries and tensions over regional and class privilege, frictions that the Portuguese constantly tried to exploit. In its realism, the book offers a historical case study for a vital question in contemporary political discourse: When privilege exists, what is the moral responsibility of those who hold it?

The Moon Will Not Burn Us

 makes clear how staggering the individual cost of collective struggle can be. By and large, the revolution was fought by kids and teenagers who never had the chance to discover who they were before the historic weight of a national movement for independence decided for them. Once, when he heard that Carmen Pereira was reluctant to leave her children for a mission to the Soviet Union, Cabral asked her, “Who do you love more: your country or your children?” Pereira eventually answered, “My homeland.”

Postcolonial African societies today may no longer face formal imperial rule, but the fight for justice, dignity, and self-determination is far from over. Oppressive systems persist through deeply entrenched forms of economic, social, political, and psychological control and exploitation. Beyond its account of women’s participation in the independence struggle, Shryock’s book reminds us that true liberation is never achieved only by tearing down an old order. It also requires the rigorous, daily work of creating a more just world in its place.

author: Keith Ang'ana
title: Kenya’s litmus test
content:
Kenya has a long and uneasy relationship with the Finance Bill. Every year, the Treasury returns with its plans for raising revenue, setting out the sums the country needs and the measures through which it hopes to collect them. On paper, these are questions of budgets and tax policy. In practice, they shape the terms of everyday life: what food costs, what it takes to keep a business running, how much remains in a payslip after deductions, and how far a household’s income can stretch.

The events of 2024 changed the way this conversation unfolded. Opposition to the Finance Bill grew into a nationwide protest movement, culminating in the breach of Parliament on June 25 and the eventual withdrawal of the bill. But the retreat was less an ending than a pause: some of its proposals would find their way back through the 

Tax Laws

, Tax Procedures, Public Finance, and Business Laws Bills of 2024.

The 2025 Finance Bill emerged in the aftermath of the 2024 protests, with the government under pressure to raise revenue without reigniting public anger over taxation. The Treasury presented its proposals largely as measures to improve compliance and close loopholes, but the bill also proposed substantive changes to Value Added Tax (VAT) exemptions and other tax provisions that could increase costs for businesses and consumers. The proposed measures were expected to raise approximately KSh 25–35 billion in additional revenue.

By 2026, the pressure to raise revenue had not eased. The government was still grappling with public debt and a difficult economic climate, while households and businesses faced the question of how much more they could absorb. The proposed tax measures were projected to generate approximately KSh 98.9 billion in additional revenue, largely through administrative reforms, tax base expansion, and improved compliance. The bill sparked debate over a proposed increase in mobile phone excise duty from 10 percent to 25 percent, potential VAT changes affecting digital payment services, and proposed taxes on 

mitumba

 imports. Other concerns centered on VAT exemptions for locally manufactured goods, access to taxpayer data by the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), and the effect of proposed tax changes on workers’ take-home pay.

In a live lecture, Churchill Ogutu helps make sense of the Finance Bill 2026, taking its figures and proposals out of the language of legislation and placing them in their wider economic context. The government’s revised tax revenue target rises from about KSh 2.6 trillion in FY26 to KSh 2.86 trillion in FY27, with the Finance Bill expected to generate 

approximately KSh 98.9 billion

 in additional revenue from the proposed tax measures.

On May 21, 2026, four days before the deadline for public submissions on the bill, Churchill Ogutu delivered a lecture to 

Bunge la Mayut

 on the Finance Bill 2026. He set out the budget cycle and revenue targets behind the bill, then walked through its proposed amendments to seven tax laws — the Income Tax Act, the Value Added Tax Act, the Excise Duty Act, the Tax Procedures Act, the Miscellaneous Fees and Levies Act, the Stamp Duty Act, and the road maintenance levy — before fielding questions from Keith Ang’ana on the 25 percent excise duty on mobile phones, the taxation of retained profits as deemed dividends, the powers of the Kenya Revenue Authority, and the prospects for PAYE relief. A cleaned transcript follows. Shilling figures are converted to US dollars at approximately KSh 129.5 to the dollar, the prevailing rate at the time, and rounded. Submissions closed on May 25. The National Assembly passed the bill on June 18, and President William Ruto signed it into law on June 23, after MPs dropped some of its most contentious proposals, including the increase in excise duty on mobile phones.

Churchill Ogutu is head of research at Capital A Investment Bank, which he joined in April 2026 after more than 15 years in financial markets in Kenya and across Africa. He was previously an economist in IC Group’s pan-African asset management division and head of research at Genghis Capital, and is an advisor at Plato Group, a global economic and political advisory firm. He holds a BSc in actuarial science from the University of Nairobi and is a member of the Economists Society of Kenya. Keith Ang’ana is a writer based in Nairobi and the founder of Bunge la Mayut. He is a co-founder of Qwani, a youth literary publication meant to publish the works of young writers.

Read a transcript of the lecture below and watch it back 

here

.

Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Churchill Ogutu. I’m the head of research at Capital A Investment Bank, and it’s a pleasure to be the guest lecturer for today’s Bunge la Mayut session. We’ll be discussing issues around the Finance Bill 2026. It’s a topical issue now that we’re getting toward the end of the budget cycle, and I’m happy to be here. It’s quite an interesting opportunity — and quite weird, just being alone and delivering this. I’m used to one-on-one interviews, but nonetheless, we’ll take it up.

Capital A Investment Bank is one of the leading investment banks, and as head of research I look at these issues, so I’m happy to give my two cents on the Finance Bill 2026. Today we’ll be looking at the context of the bill, and then at the different tax laws that are proposed to be amended, whether through insertions or the repeal of provisions in the existing tax laws. There are seven tax-related laws we’ll be looking at: the Income Tax Act, the Value Added Tax Act, the Excise Duty Act, the Miscellaneous Fees and Levies Act, the Tax Procedures Act, the Stamp Duty Act, and the road maintenance levy. Some of them are quite bulky, others not so much, but work with me within the context of this lecture.

To start us off, we need to look at the context of the Finance Bill. The Finance Bill conversation does not happen in a vacuum; there is a context that takes us to it. We have what you call the budget cycle, which started all the way back in August last year. The tabling of the Finance Bill 2026 in Parliament is pretty much taking us toward the tail end of that budget cycle. I think most people are used to seeing the Cabinet Secretary for the National Treasury with that briefcase on budget day, but the process starts a couple of months before we get there, and the uploading of the Finance Bill to the website some two weeks back is part and parcel of it.

So right now, after the tabling of the Finance Bill, we are undergoing public participation. We have until next week Monday, May 25, by 5 p.m., to give our submissions on the Finance Bill — and in the same breath, we also have to give our submissions on the budget estimates [Submissions closed on May 25, 2026. The bill was signed into law on June 23]. Because if you think about it, the budget is two sides of the same coin. On one side are the expenditure estimates, and on the other side is how we fund that expenditure. That’s where the Finance Bill comes in. It’s like at home: you have your budget, and you have to fund it. There are expenses you have to clear — maybe rent, maybe the shopping for the house, other things — but on the other side, you also have to finance that expenditure. That’s typically how even the national budget works: two sides. In this lecture we’ll be focusing our attention on the Finance Bill, but how does it fit into the bigger picture?

On the expenditure side, the story is what the government will spend in the next financial year. The financial year runs from July 1 to June 30 the following year. For that financial year, budget expenditure is around 4.8 trillion shillings (about $37 billion) — that’s what the government estimates it will spend. Revenue is around 3.6 trillion (about $28 billion), and the balance that has to be filled somehow comes to around 1.1 trillion (about $8.5 billion). Then there’s what we call nominal GDP.

Nominal GDP is the size of the economy over that financial year. For Kenya it’s around 20.8 trillion (about $161 billion), and it’s expected to grow by around 11.7 percent from the financial year that ends next month, in June. So the government’s assumption is that the economy grows by that amount. As the economy grows, expenses have to grow, and revenue collection grows too, because revenue is collected on the basis that the economy is growing. In addition, there are proposals the government makes to tweak the existing tax laws.

The next slide gives an overview of the tax revenue expected to be collected in the next financial year. It’s increasing by around 258 billion (about $2 billion) from the estimates for the current financial year. Among the line items, income tax is expected to grow by around 116 or 117 billion (about $900 million). There’s also some increase in excise duty, import duty, and VAT. Within this 258 billion, the government has said what it intends to collect from the new revenue-raising measures — that is, the Finance Bill, which we’ll be speaking about in the rest of the lecture — and from what we call the EAC customs measures. The countries within the East African Community (EAC), whose financial year also starts on July 1, do some revisions each year. Collectively, we’re expecting to raise 120 billion (about $930 million). So of the 258 billion, 120 billion is coming from the new revenue-raising measures, and the balance is basically from tightening administrative measures — increasing the compliance rate, using digital platforms to widen the tax base, things like that — and from the fact that, as I mentioned on the last slide, the economy is expected to grow by around 11 percent. They’re expecting that as the economy grows, they’ll be able to raise additional revenue from that. That’s pretty much the breakdown of the tax revenue.

The rest of the lecture focuses on the specific proposals contained in the Finance Bill 2026, starting with the income tax proposals. What’s the genesis of income tax? Individuals earn income in one form or another — salaries, or if you’re in consultancy, that’s a form of income that is also subject to tax. Businesses, too: the profits from businesses are typically subject to tax, and there’s a wide array of other income coming from corporates. So, my youths, in terms of income tax, this is the law that covers the income that comes in — either to a person from the work you do, or the profit a business makes, which is subject to corporate tax or another form of income tax. The government has looked at the existing Income Tax Act and is making some amendments. Remember, the last slide targeted increasing income tax by 116 billion (about $900 million), so one way of doing that is first to look at where they can raise the revenue from. So in the Finance Bill they’ve looked at the Income Tax Act and identified where the changes are to be made, and those are the income tax proposals we’ll be getting into now.

The first page looks at some of the definitions, because first and foremost, every law defines its terms so that people are clear what the tax law is all about. That’s section two of the Income Tax Act. A number of definitions have been targeted to be redefined or included afresh — issues such as immovable property.

There are two clauses in reference to that, so they are combining them so as to reduce the ambiguity that was there. There’s also the aspect of management or professional fees, which will now include interchange fees and merchant service fees arising from transactions that use a card as a means of payment. Bottom line: the people who provide card payments, or payments made via a card, will now be included under what we call management or professional fees. People have cards — you go to the bank, you do your transactions with whatever card you have — and up until now, that’s just classified as doing your transaction through a card. But under this Finance Bill proposal, going forward, the transactions around cards will be considered a management or professional fee. That is at the heart of this particular amendment.

Royalty has also been defined, but the proposal is now to widen the scope of what comes into royalty, specifically targeting businesses within the digital space. There’s a vibrancy around that sector, so the Finance Bill is targeting to widen the definition of royalty.

Then there’s winnings and withdrawals, being redefined in the context of income tax. This proposal is looking at segregating what is winnings and what is withdrawals — this is about betting. Traditionally, the last number of finance bills have been trying to widen the tax net toward the betting sector, so there’s been a raft of proposals around what counts as winnings. Say you place a bet, and then you win and eventually get 300 bob (about $2.30) — is the winnings that 300 bob, or is it what you had put in before? And then they’ve also brought in withdrawals: you’ve placed your bet, you’ve won, but what actually are you withdrawing, and through which platform? So the changes here are particularly about clarifying your income.

Then on the pension side: just clarifying that gratuity for a contract of service for a continuous period of at least three years is not a gain or profit. Some of the things being introduced in the Finance Bill are just cleanups of confusion around a particular clause, and the purpose is essentially to redefine and clarify the actual import of what the law is all about.

There’s a proposal on non-residential rental income tax. If you look at the way the law is currently, there is a withholding tax at a rate of 30 percent on immovable property — immovable property being, obviously, houses, land, and so on. So there’s a 30 percent withholding tax on those houses so long as the owner is not resident in Kenya. What the bill is proposing is that this non-residential rental income tax, which is currently a withholding tax, becomes a final tax. But we need some clarity, because there’s the rental income tax that we know as Kenyans, which is around 7.5 percent. That is rental income tax; it is not a withholding tax. Whereas for non-residents, rental income tax is a withholding tax. So there’s some confusion, because the way the law is currently, it’s subject to withholding tax, and yet they’ve now brought this proposal to impose a non-residential rental income tax. That’s something we’ll find out more about in the coming days as public participation continues.

There are some other proposals here, like the inclusion of the sale of scrap metal, and also winnings, within the context of management or professional fees, royalties, interest, and rents. That’s something for people dealing in scrap metal.

So they’re trying to bring that within the ambit of management or professional fees. I’ll rush through the next slide because it’s quite detailed. Here we’re looking at employees of the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) getting some relief in the event they get a loan from the CBK not exceeding 360,000 (about $2,800) for the purpose of constructing, purchasing, or improving a house occupied by the employee. So in the computation of tax for a CBK employee, 360,000 of that loan will be allowed as a deduction — like a relief for CBK employees, so long as it’s for a house the employee lives in themselves, not for rental. Those are the provisions that allow you to enjoy this particular benefit.

The other aspect is country-by-country filing. They realized there was some confusion around what you call the ultimate parent entity. Multinationals operate in different countries, so there’s a requirement for country-by-country filing, and there’s also a master file framework. This proposal in the Finance Bill is bringing clarity, because there was confusion between the master file and the country-by-country report. The proposal says that a multinational with revenue of around 9.7 billion (about $75 million) — that’s the threshold — now needs to be filing country-by-country rather than a master file. So that’s some cleanup, and there are some aspects still to be known going forward.

There’s also some cleanup on insurance funds in terms of definitions: “life insurance fund” is being replaced by “statutory fund.” If you look at the Insurance Act, what it recognizes is statutory funds, but within the Income Tax Act we have what’s called a life insurance fund. So there’s a cleanup to ensure consistency in terms of what is chargeable for tax purposes, which is the statutory fund.

Now to section 24 of the Income Tax Act, and this has really generated heat over the last couple of days: this thing called avoidance of tax liability by non-distribution of dividends. You have a company. You make revenue from your sales, you pay your expenses, and then you have the profit. Ideally, if you have shareholders, you are meant to distribute part of that as dividends. But you can retain it — not distribute it, not pay out the shareholders — to expand the business. That’s what we call retained earnings. This proposal says the KRA or the Treasury have realized that some people are avoiding tax liability by not paying the dividends they are supposed to pay to shareholders. When you have retained earnings, there’s a legitimate case for paying out part of the income as dividends, but you’re not paying. So the proposal is that at least 60 percent of that part of the income is now considered a deemed dividend. If you’ve not paid out this amount that ordinarily you should be paying as dividends, at least 60 percent of that income is considered a dividend, and you have to pay tax on that dividend.

For example: you’ve made 1 million shillings (about $7,700) in income in a year, expenses are around 600,000 (about $4,600), and hypothetically 400,000 (about $3,100) is what you’ve made.

If you have not apportioned part of that income as retained earnings, it’s deemed that you have to pay that entire 400,000 as dividends — you have to distribute it to the shareholders. What this proposal says is that at least 60 percent of the 400,000 remaining, which is 240,000 (about $1,850), will be deemed to have been paid out as dividends, so 240,000 is what will be liable to tax. We’ve had lots of debate around that: it says “at least” 60 percent, so it’s discretionary — it could go from 60 percent to 80 percent to 100 percent. That’s what’s been quite contentious over the last couple of days. But anyway, we’ll be able to get more clarity going forward.

The other aspect as we move along is section 52. Section 52 of the current Income Tax Act says that filing of returns is by June 30. If your year of income is 2025, ideally you should be filing a return by June 30 for the income you got last year. But from July 1 going forward — technically for the 2026 year of income — if this proposal sails through, it means that from next year, rather than June 30, the deadline for filing returns has been brought forward to April 30. And if you are filing a nil return for this year, you have to file by January 31 next year.

Let me be the devil’s advocate here. We heard the National Treasury saying: you already know your return. Even right now, in the month of May, we know the income that employees generated, because employees already have their salary information by now. So why should you wait until June 30 to file and clog the system? If you don’t have a business, and you typically don’t earn any income, you file a nil return — so why wait until June 30? Just do it by January 31, because it’s already a nil return. That’s the National Treasury’s argument. But the counterargument is that people are saying: Wait a minute, in instances where I need to get my financials audited, that takes a while. I also need to engage my regulator — some organizations have regulators — and the board also needs to approve. So it’s a lengthier process, and filing returns in April is a bit too soon because of all the processes that have to be followed. That’s the counterargument to the proposed amendment to section 52. The other amendment is that the return of income is to be furnished to the KRA — I think that one is clear enough.

Let’s move to the First Schedule amendments. Basically, capital gains relating to the transfer of property to a real estate investment trust (REIT) will now be exempt from tax. If you have a property, or you want to own property, ownership can happen either by building the property yourself — which is quite cumbersome, probably billions of shillings — or you can come to the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), where there are products like real estate investment trusts, and buy a unit of a building. Rather than buying the entire building, you’re getting ownership of that building through units. On capital gains: if you want to transfer your property, say a building you own, into a real estate investment trust, that transfer triggers what we call a capital gains issue, and as a result you are subject to capital gains tax.

But this proposal is coming in and saying: No, wait a minute, we shall exempt that tax, so that we improve the offering at the Nairobi Securities Exchange — so that if you’re a young person with some money, you can put it into a real estate investment trust, because currently such transfers complicate things. If you have a property and you can put it within the control of a real estate investment trust without the transfer attracting a tax burden, that should increase the pool of things people can invest in. I think that’s the purpose of this particular proposal.

The other proposal is around some clarity on industrial buildings in terms of investment allowance. There wasn’t a rate for it. If you’ve built an industrial building, the allowance lets you get some relief over the next, say, ten years — but there wasn’t a rate for that relief. Say you’ve built an industrial building worth 1 billion shillings (about $7.7 million). Technically, you should be able to deduct it in terms of investment allowance, meaning that when you’re calculating your taxes, you get some form of relief for a number of years as you recoup your investment. Typically, the investment allowance is there to encourage investment. But there was no rate. Now the Finance Bill says the rate will be 10 percent. So for that 1 billion, in equal installments over the next ten years, KSh 100 million (about $770,000) a year will be like a relief that helps you recover your investment over those ten years.

There are a number of other proposals here — for example, a reduction of the income tax rate for non-resident contractors in the extractive industries. In the extractives, especially with the noise we’ve been hearing about rare earth minerals in some parts of the country, we’ve seen that most of the people coming in are foreigners, not locals. Because of that, the income tax rate for non-resident contractors within the extractive sector is being reduced — right now it’s at 7.5 percent and it’s being reduced to 30 percent — to boost some of these investments. But at the same time, as they come into Kenya, into rare earths and the extractives, there’s what you call repatriated income: The profits they make, they take back to the countries they came from. So there’s an introduction of a 15 percent tax on that income they take back to the parent countries. That is a brief summary of the income tax proposals — quite a number of them, but to me, that covers income tax.

The other aspect is value-added tax (VAT). VAT is basically on the consumption of goods and services: If you purchase a good or procure a service, there’s a VAT element to that purchase. There’s a Value Added Tax Act in Kenya that deals with that. Say you go to buy stuff — a commodity, you go to the shop, you buy vegetables at the supermarket — or you go for services and you get a service. There are VAT-able items: the things you buy within the context of the standard VAT rate of 16 percent that you have to pay. When you buy those things, or services, there’s VAT on them. That’s the heart of the next set of proposals, on VAT.

The first one starts at section two. Section two of all the tax laws looks at the definitions. Here it’s basically deleting some definitions: assessment, information technology, and tax computerized system. These are things that exist within the context of VAT.

But if you go and look at the Tax Procedures Act, it also speaks to these things. So the Finance Bill is saying that if they are within the context of VAT, they should be removed, since they’re already in the Tax Procedures Act — rather than having duplication, they should sit within the Tax Procedures Act and be removed from VAT. That’s the import of the amendments we’re seeing to section two.

There are quite a number of things here, but one notable one is section 31 of the VAT Act, which speaks about refund of tax on bad debt. Say you sell to someone and you expect them to pay, including some VAT — you expect the payment, but eventually they don’t pay. The proposal is revising the timeline for the relief: It’s being pushed by another year, from two years to three years. The impact is that it will delay access to VAT refunds — rather than claiming within two years, you start claiming within three years — and potentially it could lead to cash flow issues, because maybe you were depending on that refund, but now it’s being pushed further down the road. That will lead to cash flow issues for businesses seeking refunds from the KRA.

The other issue is tax avoidance schemes. As I said, there are definitions being removed from VAT because they are already within the Tax Procedures Act (TPA), and that also applies to this particular proposal. There is a clause, section 66, which touches on tax avoidance schemes for the purposes of VAT, but there’s another proposal within the Tax Procedures Act that deals specifically with tax avoidance schemes. So that’s the cleanup — to remove it from VAT and put it within the Tax Procedures Act. That’s the proposal we’re seeing.

Another thing is around tax invoices. Right now there’s section 42, and the requirement to issue a tax invoice deals specifically with registered persons — so if you have revenue of at least KSh 5 million (about $39,000) in a given year, you are supposed to register within this ambit of a tax invoice. But now the proposal is removing “registered,” so that it remains as “persons.” It’s saying you don’t need to be a registered person; irrespective of whether you’ve registered or not, for the purposes of issuing a tax invoice, it’s for everyone. My interpretation is that this is an extended requirement, not just for people within the VAT regime but for everyone — you and me. That’s something which will be quite interesting to see if it sails through.

Then we get to the First Schedule of the VAT Act, which looks at exempt items. Exempt means that when you deliver or produce a good, you can go back and claim on some of the inputs you used. Let me give an example. Assume you’re a registered baker. You need flour, you need cooking oil, you need certain things to produce bread. So yes, you can produce bread, but at the same time, the flour and the oil you used, which you paid VAT on when you bought them — if they’re exempt, it means you can claim back the VAT you paid on the inputs you used to make the bread. That’s the upshot of what is exempt. But there’s a proposal here to move some items from exempt status to the standard rate of 16 percent.

So we have items that were under exempt status being moved to the standard rate: spacecraft; goods and services for direct and exclusive use in the construction of tourism facilities; the supply of denatured ethanol; items like direction-finding compasses, instruments, and appliances for aircraft — that’s for people with aircraft, it’s applicable to them; and spare parts imported or purchased for direct and exclusive use in the implementation of official aid projects. Initially these were exempt; now they’re being moved to the standard rate, so 16 percent will be applicable to these products.

Then there are items moving from the standard rate of 16 percent to exempt status — a number of products, but for the purposes of this lecture, the ones we’ll touch on. Scrap metal, which is at 16 percent but is being moved to exempt status — remember, under income tax we touched on the issue of scrap metal, but this is a different thing. The supply of imported or locally purchased telephones for cellular networks and other wireless networks — if you have a business importing or locally purchasing telephones, that’s currently at 16 percent VAT, but it’s being moved to an exempt category. Another item is worn clothing and other worn articles of tariff heading 6309, other than importation — there’s a buzzing industry for repurposing secondhand clothes, at the export processing zones (EPZs) for instance, and this excludes the importation. These were at 16 percent but are being moved to exempt status. Then there’s the supply of goods or services in the implementation of infrastructure projects undertaken within public-private partnerships (PPPs). There are projects being implemented under PPP — quite a number of them. I think the Rironi–Mau Summit road — yes, that’s a PPP project. And there are other projects in the pipeline. If you are delivering goods or services to any of these projects being implemented under PPP, what was 16 percent will be exempt. That’s something to spur some of the infrastructure projects, and it’s effective from July 1 if this proposal sails through.

There’s also a raft of proposals moving things from zero-rated to exempt. Zero-rated goods are those where, technically, the justification is that on one hand you have inputs, as with our bakery example, but at the same time you don’t have any justification whatsoever to push this cost to consumers. So for these goods, it’s 0 percent VAT. But now there’s a proposal to move some of these from zero-rating status to exempt status. The transportation of sugar cane from farms to milling factories was zero-rated but is being moved to exempt status. The supply of electric bicycles — at least in Nairobi you see a number of these operators; I think this is a reference to the electric motorcycles coming up, quite a number of them — will move from zero-rated to exempt status if this passes. And there’s a whole host of raw materials, locally purchased or imported, for the manufacture of artificial animal feeds, moving from zero-rated to exempt.

Okay, I think we’ve finished with value-added tax. First it was income tax, then VAT, and now we move to excise duty. There are certain products which have a specific rate of tax applicable to them. Back in the day, we used to know it as a sin tax. When excise duty came, it was a sin tax, in the sense that these taxes were brought in as prohibitive measures for tobacco, beer, and all those kinds of things. That’s how we used to know it. But is it still a sin tax? If you look at the ambit of the goods within excise duty, quite a number of them — non-alcoholic drinks and some other goods which are not necessarily bad. The difference here is that VAT touches on goods and services in a broader sense.

Either you are zero-rated, standard-rated, or exempt — or a rate which is neither standard nor zero, like petroleum at 8 percent VAT, somewhere in between. But when you look at the excise duty regime, it’s different, because it’s looking at specific goods, and then there’s a specific tax rate for each of them. Traditionally these were sin taxes, but now it’s been widened.

Section two of the Excise Duty Act seeks to add antique, vintage, or classic vehicles, so there’s a definition for that. That means that further down the line, there’s a specific tax rate applicable to these vehicles. That was the notable amendment to section two — to define what these vehicles are.

Now, this is a hot one. There’s a new section, section 6A: imposition of excise duty on locally purchased or imported telephones upon activation. Interesting. Some have made noise about it, because right now, in the context of excise duty, it’s typically upon importation — as you import goods, that’s the point where excise duty or VAT is applicable. But now we’re seeing that upon activation of a phone, locally purchased or imported, the point at which you’re activating it is where you’re paying this particular excise. That’s a new section 6A of the Excise Duty Act being introduced.

Further down, section 36 of the Excise Duty Act: payment of excise duty on cellular phones. So section 6A is saying that there will be an imposition of excise duty — from July 1, if this passes through, there’ll be duty upon activation of a phone that is either locally purchased or imported — and then section 36 speaks to the payment of excise duty on cellular phones. It’s an additional provision: Section 36 speaks about what is subject to excise duty, so it basically says there’ll be a payment of excise duty on cellular phones, bringing alive this new section 6A. Then if you go to the First Schedule, it says that 25 percent excise duty on imported cellular phones will be applicable. This particular clause takes effect from January 2027.

There are a number of other amendments too — the various rates of excise duty for antique, vintage, or classic vehicles. It’ll be 50 percent of the excisable value. So if you have an antique car — say a 1950s car — with an excisable value of KSh 1 million (about $7,700), the proposed law says you have to pay excise duty of 50 percent of that: KSh 500,000 (about $3,900) on that vintage.

So we go to the next broad proposal, the Tax Procedures Act. So far, those were the explicit taxes, but now we get to the procedures, because there are procedures for how you pay taxes, and there’s a specific law that tackles those procedures. That’s the Tax Procedures Act, and various amendments have been brought into play. Section two speaks about the deletion of “certificate of origin” and the insertion of “virtual asset service provider.” Sometime last year, we saw the Virtual Asset Service Providers Bill being passed, so it’s now an act of Parliament. Basically, it brings to the fore the fact that virtual assets are quite significant in the economy: Bitcoin, forex, digital lending within the virtual asset space, and all that. So there’s a definition of virtual asset service provider in line with that act of Parliament that was passed last year.

Then there’s a new section 6C, which still touches on virtual asset service providers — how they file information returns. They’ve assessed that Kenya is becoming more of a digital economy with all these virtual assets, so now that we have the virtual asset service providers, this is how they need to go about filing information returns. There’s also section 6D, which speaks about agreements for the automatic exchange of information with other countries on virtual asset transactions. Some transactions in the virtual asset space cut across borders, so this proposal says Kenya can now share information with other countries that have implemented this framework, to assess transactions within the virtual asset space. That’s tied to recognizing that there’s a Virtual Asset Service Providers Act in place, and trying to fine-tune how they can better target that space.

There’s the section 10 amendment on deregistration. If for one reason or another you are deregistered in terms of your PIN — you have a PIN, but you’re deregistered — then in the event that you re-register, you can still get back the same PIN, because everyone has a unique PIN number. At least it enhances continuity, because they have your records. It’s easier than having two different PINs, one up until the point you were deregistered and another new one. It ensures continuity of your tax records if you re-register after deregistration.

There’s another one, section 12 of the Tax Procedures Act. I’m within that space, in the investment bank. Right now, one of the requirements for non-residents is that they need to have a PIN as one of the know-your-customer (KYC) documentation requirements. But the Finance Bill is saying that investment banks will no longer require them to have a PIN. It’s reducing compliance costs, because it’s quite lengthy to get a PIN — I’d experienced it previously, with some foreign investors coming in to acquire a PIN; it’s a lengthy process. This one is giving a reprieve, to spur foreign investors coming into the Nairobi Securities Exchange.

Tax avoidance schemes: As we said, this was in section 66 of the VAT Act, but now there’s a new section 18A of the Tax Procedures Act that brings alive these tax avoidance schemes. So they repeal section 66 of the VAT Act and bring in a new clause under the Tax Procedures Act.

There’s another new one, quite interesting: a new section 29A, whereby the KRA — in this case the commissioner — can issue its own assessment. Right now, section 29 of the Tax Procedures Act gives a person the leeway to self-assess. But this new proposal says that over and above you as an individual conducting your self-assessment, the KRA can now come in and issue an assessment independently. There’s some concern that they’ll be overstepping their mandate, going over and above what they are required to do. That’s quite concerning, but we’ll see. We’ve had lots of noise around that.

The other aspect, which is quite an interesting one, is the tax amnesty. In the event that, for one reason or another, you’ve not paid your taxes, there’s normally some interest and some fines that you’re supposed to pay over and above the tax.

Tax amnesty basically waives all those fines and penalties — just pay the tax you’re supposed to pay. The last tax amnesty, which ran through June last year, was on the tax for the year of income ending December 2023. Now this has been extended up to last year, and you have until the end of December to pay the outstanding tax you did not pay for last year, without incurring the penalties and fees. That’s the tax amnesty. As we mentioned earlier, this tax amnesty is expected to yield KSh 30 billion (about $230 million); the last one yielded KSh 50 billion (about $390 million). It brings about an issue of moral hazard: as a taxpayer, I know that at some point the KRA or the National Treasury will come with a tax amnesty, so why should I pay the tax right now? A year or two down the line, I can benefit from a tax amnesty without incurring penalties or fines. That’s an issue coming up with this proposal to extend the tax amnesty.

There are a number of other proposals here. Section 75: The KRA may use the electronic tax system to generate pre-populated tax returns. Going forward, they’ll be able to introduce pre-populated returns in the self-assessment system, so if the KRA brings in this IT system, you’ll be able to generate pre-populated returns, and the assessment is then just going through them and confirming whether they make sense.

There’s also the repeal of the certificate of origin. One of the things we spoke about at the beginning was the definition of certificate of origin being entirely shelved, because the focus on the certificate of origin will no longer be within the Tax Procedures Act but within the East African Community Customs Management Act. That’s the whole point of repealing the definition in section two, and then section 44A repeals the certificate of origin itself. Pretty much a cleanup, to ensure that anything to do with certificates of origin is handled from a customs perspective. There are others — section 86 being replaced with a new section dealing with failure to comply with the electronic tax system, a whole host of things — but by and large, we’re pretty much done with the Tax Procedures Act.

Next we move to miscellaneous fees and levies — two or three proposals here. The first is the reduction of fees paid into the fund from 20 percent to 10 percent. There’s the import declaration fee, and a portion of it ends up in a fund, the Import Declaration Fee Fund. Initially, the portion of the fees that went into this fund was 20 percent, but the proposal is to reduce it to 10 percent. Then section nine deals with the East African Community Customs Management Act. Initially, the import declaration fee, the railway development levy, and the export levy were within the ambit of the EAC Customs Management Act, but now the proposal is to delete that reference. It means that the other levies, which did not eventually end up within the context of the East African Community, will now be included, because initially they had restricted it to just the import declaration fee, the railway development levy, and the export levy. With the deletion, whatever levies are collected will now eventually end up within the context of customs.

Coming to the tail end is the stamp duty. As we mentioned earlier with real estate investment trusts: You have a property you want to transfer, and under the income tax proposals the capital gains tax on that was exempted.

So section 96A now specifically includes instruments that transfer interest in property to a real estate investment trust. If you have a property and you want to transfer it to a REIT, that instrument will now be included within the context of stamp duty — I think just to spur the transfers we’re seeing. If you have a property and you want it included within a REIT, a stamp duty proposal is coming in to redefine it.

Lastly, the road maintenance levy, which is collected through the purchase of petroleum products, petrol and diesel. A bit of it goes into the roads annuity fund. Right now, we are paying 25 shillings (about 19 US cents) per liter as road maintenance levy, and three shillings (about 2 cents) of that goes into the roads annuity fund. The proposal is to reduce what goes to the roads annuity fund from three shillings to one shilling and 50 cents (about 1 US cent). Largely, this is what you call appropriations-in-aid, so it doesn’t have a bearing on the tax revenue we spoke about.

That’s a snapshot of the Finance Bill — quite lengthy, quite detailed. I hope I’ve done it justice in slightly over an hour. It’s my first time just giving a lecture like this, quite an interesting one. Anyway, you can now submit your written memorandum to the Clerk of the National Assembly; there’s an email there that you can see. You can also submit to the Finance Committee of the National Assembly; there’s an email there too. The deadline is next Monday, May 25, by 5 p.m. East Africa Time. There’s no extension, for sure — Kenyans, I know you with extensions. There’s no extension. By 5 p.m. you need to submit your memorandum on the bill. Thanks.

Keith Ang'ana

Thank you very much, Mr. Churchill. That was an amazing presentation, and it has been very enlightening, because the thing about the Finance Bill is that it’s a very tough document to go through, especially because you need to compare it with the previous acts — the Income Tax Act, the VAT Act — and it’s a very tedious thing. But you have been able to break it down for us, and we’ve been able to understand it. So first of all, thank you very much for that. You made it look easy.

Before we release you, there are a couple of questions that have come out of the discussion, and we’d like to put them to you so that you can shed some clarity, so that we understand as we go ahead to make our public participation submissions.

First of all, just a general question, an overview. Do you have an opinion on how this bill compares to last year’s Finance Bill? Is it fair to the citizens, or does it lean more toward the government in terms of collecting more revenue?

Churchill Ogutu

An apples-to-apples comparison will be slightly hard — I may not do it justice. If you look at what was targeted to be collected last year, I think it was KSh 35 billion (about $270 million) in the initial Finance Bill proposal. This time we have KSh 54 billion (about $420 million) that is targeted to be collected, and there’s another KSh 30 billion (about $230 million) from the tax amnesty. So the proposal this time around seems to be quite aggressive. And there are other aspects on the procedures — for instance, the filing, which we now need to front-load, rather than filing by June 30 the way we know it, bringing it two months earlier to April 30. Ostensibly, from what you hear, that gives the KRA some time to do reconciliations and all that, but obviously it will increase compliance costs, if you think about how people will try to implement this. Those are some of the things that stood out for me in the bill.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay. And just generally, as an economist, do you think that the more taxes are increased, the less the government possibly collects? Because from the Finance Bill 2024, there was this issue of the Laffer curve, whereby the government is trying to be more aggressive and increase regulations, but in the end, when the quarterly reports come out, the KRA usually misses its target. So do you think it’ll possibly be the same now, with the introduction of these many amendments on taxes?

Churchill Ogutu

If you look at it from where I started, the tax revenue target, if you compare where we are right now, the supplementary budget, with what is being targeted in the next financial year, there’s an increase of KSh 258 billion (about $2 billion), of which KSh 120 billion (about $930 million) is coming from this Finance Bill and the EAC tax amendments, which are also part of the Finance Bill. The balance, they say, will come either from tightening administrative measures, or they’re just banking on the economy continuing to boom, so that revenue will continue. Remember that you still have the existing tax laws as they are. The Finance Bill, the 57 clauses, is just seeing avenues for other revenue measures.

Out of these KSh 258 billion (about $2 billion), KSh 120 billion (about $930 million) is coming from these new measures. So they’re also hoping that what they collected this financial year, ending in June — however little it is — continues. But already, looking at the numbers up to April and comparing them to where they ideally should be, it points to the fact that they might miss the target. There’s another aspect, what you call tax buoyancy: You look at the percentage growth in tax revenue against the percentage growth in nominal GDP. If the growth in revenues is more than the growth in GDP, that means they can meet their revenue target. But the numbers for the next financial year show that number is below one — it’s 0.7 — so the assumption is that the economy is growing faster than they can collect revenue.

A number of things feed into that. You’re largely looking at the formal sector. On the individual side, you’ve seen that disposable income has pretty much shrunk. On the corporate side, the analysis even in the Economic Survey shows that, as much as profits from businesses are quite significant, they’re not growing as fast as they used to. So the taxes expected from income taxes, whether individual or corporate — or even if you look at consumption, because disposable income has shrunk, you’re not consuming as much as you used to. This feeds into the negative revenue performance we’ve seen, and it challenges the point in your question: We are doing all these tax proposals, yet we know we may not even hit the target, so why do it? It’s still a debatable issue. But ultimately, you may find they are caught in a catch-22.

Step back: We had the medium-term revenue strategy, being implemented in two phases. The first phase started in July 2024 and is supposed to end by June 2027. They’re looking at it in terms of tax revenue to GDP. When they wanted to start it off, it was 14.3 percent tax revenue to GDP; the goal was to increase it to 20 percent. That’s what they were looking at in July 2024. There were some measures in that medium-term revenue strategy which potentially could have benefited people: They were looking at reducing VAT from 16 percent gradually, possibly to 14 percent; the corporate tax rate from 30 percent to 25 percent; the PAYE top band from 35 percent to 25 percent. But we missed the boat — June 2024 happened, and it went back. So even now, they still haven’t reached there. You can pity the government that they want to reach 20 percent, but even looking at the numbers for the next financial year, we are still at 14 percent.

We haven’t even moved, even within the context of implementing this medium-term revenue strategy. So you can pity them, but you also have to be alive to the economy — the economy probably is not solid enough to support higher taxes, or these tax proposals.

Keith Ang'ana

Yes, thank you. I think that sheds more light on it. On that note, I wanted to ask some questions about the specific amendments. This is something you’ve mentioned already, but some clarity was needed on the particular point of section 6A of the Excise Duty Act, imposing a 25 percent tax on mobile phones at the time of activation. The question that’s been asked is: At what particular point in time can we say a phone is activated? Is it when it’s been imported, or when it’s turned on? How will this work?

Churchill Ogutu

I think more of the latter, at the point where you turn it on, rather than at the point of importation. Ideally this stuff happens at the point of importation, whereby as you import these goods, you have the import declaration forms and all the requisite taxes and levies you have to pay. But this time, from the look of things — or the intent of this, if it sails through — you don’t pay them at that point, but at the point of activation. And that raises legitimate concerns: What is activation?

Keith Ang'ana

And is it levied on the importer and then transferred to the buyer, or directly on the buyer? It seems like — 

Churchill Ogutu

It seems like it’s on the buyer, at the point of activation of the phone, because the buyer is the one who has to activate it.
