So it means that even the purchase price will have to go up by 25 percent, because that’s the excise duty being slapped on at the point of activation. So it’s on the buyer — the consumer, ultimately.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay. The next question, because this is something that has generated a lot of heat on Twitter: There’s section 24 of the Income Tax Act, which provides the KRA with powers to tax companies on their retained profits — something about if a company does not pay out at least 60 percent of its profits as dividends, the KRA will treat part of the remaining profit as deemed dividends and go ahead and tax it. So first of all, have you seen that part? And the question being asked is whether this would choke businesses and make them lose the incentive for which they carry out their operations, because now the KRA will also be taxing more of the profits that haven’t been paid out as dividends. So the question is: What has been the practice with the KRA and dividends, and what does that section actually mean?

Churchill Ogutu

This section brings a different interpretation of what a deemed dividend is. Initially, the wording was that they considered a portion of the income. The example I gave: You have revenues of, say, KSh 1 million (about $7,700); expenses of KSh 600,000 (about $4,600); so you have profit of, say, KSh 400,000 (about $3,100), assuming you don’t have anything other than that. Part of it you can say is retained earnings; part of it could be taken through. But the assumption here is that there’s tax avoidance, in a way, by not distributing dividends. They need to look at why you are not making dividend payments — there could be a myriad of reasons behind that — whereas the lens being used, as it is, is that whatever profit you have, you have to be paying a portion of it as dividends. The underlying assumption is that at least 60 percent of what you did not distribute is now deemed to be the dividend paid to your shareholders. But it assumes a number of things. It assumes you just have money there that ideally you should be distributing as dividends — but potentially you could be retaining it; you could be trying to expand the business, or timing investment decisions for the future. So it’s not that you have to distribute it as dividends, but the requirement, as it is in the proposal, is that you should be distributing it as dividends. Other than that, they just assume at least 60 percent of it should be treated as if it’s been distributed — which might not necessarily be the case. That’s what’s problematic about this particular proposal.

Keith Ang'ana

So when the proposal says at least 60 percent, does it mean the baseline is 60 percent and the KRA can go up, if they want, to a particular percentage?

Churchill Ogutu

Yeah, that’s the thing, because it speaks about at least 60 percent. So in the assessment they may say: We’ve looked at you, and probably it’s 100 percent that you disbursed as dividends, and you have to pay tax on that distributed dividend — as it is, because it’s a deemed dividend. Ultimately, the KRA is the one coming in and saying 100 percent is what you distributed to your shareholders, when probably you didn’t even distribute to shareholders. But that’s the assumption this particular proposal is hinging on.

Keith Ang'ana

Just based on that: There’s the problem of how the KRA has been given more interventionary powers to audit people’s accounts, including their banks and their M-Pesa, to demand tax, and to punish non-compliance with fines. Do you think it’s advisable to give the tax body these powers?

Churchill Ogutu

I think, by and large, the KRA already has the necessary tools to conduct whatever audit they might want on a taxpayer. I think this particular proposal is the one that speaks about how, over and above the self-assessment, they can independently conduct their own assessment. At least it has to be within the current framework; it shouldn’t infringe on your privacy. The moment it goes into that, it negates data protection — because time and again, finance bills bring up this issue around data protection, with the KRA coming in and infringing on the data protection laws we enjoy as Kenyans. Ultimately it has to be within a certain framework. I believe they can’t assess unless they come up with some tools — I don’t know what tools they’re looking at to do assessments. But I think they might be targeting some of these other professionals, in my view, who are not within this ambit, because time and again they’ve been saying that the formally employed are the ones under personal income tax. We have other professionals — doctors, lawyers, professionals who don’t fit, who don’t get the salaries subject to this kind of personal income tax regime. So unless they want to widen the tax bracket to home in on some of these — ultimately, it has to be within a proper framework, not infringing on privacy, and within the context of data protection laws.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay, great. The next question touches on section 12 of the Tax Procedures Act, which basically states that a foreigner shall be exempt from the requirement of having a KRA PIN when opening an account with an investment bank. The question being asked is: What might be the motive for this, and might it by any chance increase the chances of fraud?

Churchill Ogutu

Ah, well, that’s at the heart of my bread and butter, because I’m an investment banker. Typically, as part of KYC, any local who opens an account with an investment bank has KYC documents required of them: a national ID, a PIN, not necessarily a bank statement, those kinds of things. Some of those also apply to foreign investors who want to invest in the Nairobi Securities Exchange — they’re required to have their passports, and they’re also required to have a PIN for the purposes of taxation. But now this is being removed. As I mentioned earlier, it tends to be a lengthy process for a foreigner to acquire a PIN in the country, so they’re just removing this compliance burden, which is part of the KYC documentation. I think it’s quite good. The motive is probably to stimulate foreign investment — or rather, foreign equity portfolio flows. Investors who invest in the Nairobi Securities Exchange are called portfolio investors, not foreign direct investors. So they want to stimulate that activity. It could be beneficial, as I said, within the investment bank — it’s something that’s quite welcome to us.

Keith Ang'ana

Something that you deal in. Okay, so it seems like we’re not done with section 24, because people still have more questions on it. The issue is that dividend distribution tax is already captured under corporate tax, meaning the income is already taxed. So does the introduction of this mean the KRA is placing a tax on top of another tax?

Churchill Ogutu

Quite an interesting one. You look at it to the extent of the businesses. I was just assuming a simple business where you have your profits, and then you can declare dividends — the same way Safaricom, for instance, recently declared a dividend on part of its profit. That dividend is paid from the profits. But before you get to the profits, there are the other expenses that have already been paid, which may typically exclude the payment of dividends. So in this scenario, it’s now the deemed dividend — the one they just assume you were supposed to have paid but did not pay out to your shareholders. I think that’s pretty much where they’re coming from with this proposal: this income — why haven’t you paid it as dividends? But it raises another conversation around how they’re sort of chaperoning all businesses into paying dividends as a must. Like, you have to pay dividends as a must, or the counter is that if you don’t pay dividends, it’s at the discretion of the KRA — at least 60 percent of whatever remains is now deemed as a dividend that was paid. I think that’s the heart of it.

Keith Ang'ana

Yeah, and I think you’ve just touched on this with your last statement. But the question being asked, which I think is a very tough question, is how this new change affects alignment with the Companies Act regarding dividend policy autonomy.

Churchill Ogutu

Those are the issues that come to the fore as you start implementing some of these proposals, and I think, by and large, we’ll keep hearing them in the context of the ongoing public participation, because they bring other angles that the framers of the bill potentially had not considered in the first instance. That’s why we have to give our submissions by next week Monday, to bring out some of these issues. But that’s a legitimate issue, because now you’re interfering with the dividend policy of a company.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay. We already saw a drop in the money being transacted through M-Pesa in the latest Kenya National Bureau of Statistics report. Now this Finance Bill actually proposes taxing mobile money more. Please elaborate on that section of the bill and maybe touch on its effect on people and the economy — since of course there’s a lot of digital money penetration, and we as a country are known for M-Pesa.

Churchill Ogutu

That speaks to the aspect of interchange fees — the inclusion of interchange fees, cards, and a whole array of payment platforms within the ambit of withholding tax. I think we first need to get better clarity on what the intention was, because on one hand, if you hear from the National Treasury, it’s like they’re targeting the providers of payment cards; that’s what they were keenly pursuing. Yet at the same time, mobile money payment is also part of payments — you can also make payments through virtual cards, or through mobile. So clarity needs to be sought on who is being pursued by this particular proposal. But obviously, if you look at it in the context of mobile money, assuming that will be within this ambit and subject to this withholding tax, it will definitely increase transaction costs — which I don’t think is the intention, looking at the Economic Survey data showing that transactions have somehow slowed down in the economy. As you increase transaction costs, obviously it will dampen the mobile money transactions we’re seeing in the economy.

Keith Ang'ana

The other question being asked is that Mbadi, and also President Ruto, had promised to look at the tax bands and lower PAYE — and, of course, you mentioned this within the medium-term revenue strategy — where the current top PAYE rate of 35 percent is higher than the 30 percent corporate rate, contrary to the national tax policy, which recommends that individuals should not be taxed more than companies. Is it feasible to just reduce PAYE?

Churchill Ogutu

Is it feasible to reduce PAYE? That was contained in the medium-term revenue strategy and the national tax policy: harmonizing the corporate tax, which was to be lowered from 30 percent to 25 percent, and also ensuring that the individual tax rate — the top band of PAYE — comes down from 35 percent to 25 percent. Because as it is right now, you’d rather pay the corporate tax rate, because it’s lower than the top band at 35 percent, depending on the income band you’re in. Remember this is graduated: Currently the first KSh 24,000 (about $185) is at 10 percent; the next KSh 8,333 (about $64) is at 25 percent; and then from KSh 32,333 (about $250) all the way to KSh 500,000 (about $3,900) at 30 percent, and so on. So I think they might have to do some simulations, not just look at reducing PAYE and whether it’s feasible. Because if you reduce it, it will lead to money being returned to people’s pockets, and then they’ll be able to consume more. So you’re reducing this, but you can see VAT going higher as a result. The last time, the National Treasury mentioned there are simulations ongoing.

Tied to that, speaking of zero-rating: That proposal came in around February, when we had CS Mbadi saying that the first KSh 30,000 (about $230) will be zero-rated. Remember, we don’t have a zero rate — the first KSh 24,000 (about $185) is at 10 percent; there’s no 0 percent, but we have a personal tax relief; everyone gets KSh 2,400 (about $19) in relief. So the way to think about this zero-rating: Is it that people who earn below KSh 30,000 (about $230) on a monthly basis get 0 percent? Also remember it’s a graduated scale, so if you’re earning KSh 200,000 (about $1,500), your first KSh 30,000 in this framework would be 0 percent — will it be applicable to everyone, because of the graduated scale as we know it, or will it be limited to people at or below KSh 30,000 shillings, so that they get 0 percent? And then the next band, between KSh 30,000 and KSh 50,000 (about $390), will reduce from 30 percent to 25 percent. So technically you’re jumping from 0 percent to 25 percent. And does it mean that, assuming the corporate tax rate comes down to 25 percent, everyone else. . . . ? There are a few things still up in the air; we need clarity around that.

In addition, we’ve been hearing — and I also mentioned this earlier — that they want to introduce PAYE even to some professionals who currently are not salaried employees, in consultancy or otherwise; they want to bring them within the PAYE regime. Is it that, as they do this for low-income employees — because I think the target is everyone below 50,000 (about $390), who one way or another are getting some form of relief — they now want to offset it with these professionals coming on board? Those are some of the things being worked out right now, from my sense.

But now the question is: We’ve seen the Finance Bill, and people are now doing public participation on the Finance Bill as it is. If they want to introduce this and have it passed by June 30, it means they will introduce an amendment well after the public participation stage has come and passed. We’ve been telling people they need to give their submissions by next week Monday. That closes. And then much later — because typically there’s the first reading of the bill, which is literally a first reading: This is the Finance Bill 2026, it proposes to make amendments, blah blah blah. Then it goes to the second reading stage, where there’s a report by the Departmental Committee on Finance and National Planning. This report also incorporates the public participation, and then Parliament debates the report — the merits of the current 57 proposals.

But then at the same time, it introduces some amendments before it goes to the third stage. So if this particular proposal is introduced, we’re looking at it being introduced well after the public participation has been conducted. Potentially, as I said, will they go for zero-rating, or will they — I don’t know — increase? I don’t know what modalities they’ll use. Some of them may be prohibitive, but people won’t get a chance to weigh in on them, because it will be well after the public participation. Those are the things that are still mind-boggling — how they’ll go about it. Or does it mean that, if this Finance Bill window closes, they introduce a tax amendment bill further down the line? That would be around six months from now, December thereabouts. So it’s still up in the air at this point.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay, and I think that’s a great point on which to finish up. It’s been an amazing session. Thank you very much once again. Just as we end, I want to ask you to remind us how to make our views known to Parliament. If you can take us through the submission process one last time.

Churchill Ogutu

You can submit your written memorandum — you can actually write it. I know I’m speaking to. . . .  there’s normally this debate about the millennials and the Gen Zs. So for the millennials, and those who are Gen X and all that, you can hand-deliver it to the Office of the Clerk, first floor, Main Parliament Buildings, Nairobi. You know where it is. I don’t know whether this will be applicable to other people, because this is not just a Nairobi affair; it’s also for people in other parts of the country. If you’re not able to hand-deliver your written or printed submission to the Office of the Clerk, you can send an email to the Clerk of the National Assembly, which you can see on the screen, cna@parliament.go.ke, and also to the Finance Committee, chaired by the Honorable Kuria Kimani, at financecommitteena@parliament.go.ke. The deadline is 5 p.m. next Monday, May 25 — East Africa Time. There’s no extension. By the way, that will be the day after a team in North London lifts the league. Remember: You lift the league first on Sunday, and then on Monday you submit. Whichever sequencing you want — lift the league first and then submit, or submit and then lift the league — you have to submit by next week Monday, 5 p.m. East Africa Time [Submissions have since closed. The email addresses above are given as they were shared during the lecture.].

Keith Ang'ana

Yeah, and they should look out for any public hearings that will be happening.

Churchill Ogutu

Yeah.

Keith Ang'ana

Yes, thank you very much, and I think we have come to the end of this. 

Shukran sana

.

Churchill Ogutu

Thank you for having me.

author: Fabrizio Floris
title: The Sahara was never a border
content:
In July, Algeria and Mali reinstated their ambassadors and reopened their airspace to each other, more than a year after Algerian forces shot down a Malian drone near the border town of Tin Zaouatine. 

Al Jazeera reported the thaw

; Agence France-Presse (AFP) 

added

 that rebel advances in northern Mali had accelerated it, and that restoring cross-border security cooperation was a priority. In September, Algeria’s prime minister was 

received in Bamako with military honors

. 

The reconciliation is about a border that both governments say they cannot control.

Farther east, on the Algeria–Niger frontier, the same logic works differently. The Niger-based NGO, Alarme Phone Sahara, counted more than 34,000 people 

expelled from Algeria to Niger in 2025

, a record, up from 31,404 in 2024 and 26,031 in 2023. Migrants who are not Nigerien are left at a desert spot known as Point Zéro and they walk about 15km to Assamaka.

Both stories treat the Sahara as a line to be secured: a front to be held, a space to be cleared of the wrong people. Judith Scheele’s 

Shifting Sands: A Human History of the Sahara

 (2025) is a sustained argument that this is the wrong picture. An anthropologist at the 

École des hautes études en sciences sociales

, Scheele 

combines historical archives, including many Arabic-language accounts, with decades of fieldwork

 and interviews with Saharans themselves. Edward Said taught us that places are imagined before they are governed; Fernand Braudel, that seas link as much as they divide. Scheele applies both lessons to a desert.

Scheele’s Sahara is a human world. The book moves from a city-building civilization in Libya’s Fezzan, contemporary with the Roman Empire, through the caravan trades that carried gold, salt, textiles, and enslaved people to the borderlands of Algeria, Mali, Niger, Chad, and Libya that she knows from her own travels.

The caravan of gold and spice is the image that outsiders inherited, and Scheele asks readers to separate Saharan from trans-Saharan trade: the second is the part that crosses the region and so leaves traces in archaeological sites and in sources written beyond it. Most Saharan trade, she suggests, was in staples, the cereals, dates, salt, cloth, dried meat and skins that groups such as the Arba’a and the Tubu carried. The fabled gold was something the explorer René Caillié never saw in Timbuktu.

The trade in staples survives, and it remains, in Scheele’s phrase, “relatively democratic”: anyone with a four-by-four, some capital and enough cousins along the road can become a carrier or trade on their own account, and negotiate with Malian customs officials. She also notes that the advance of trade routes, and the political rivalries that followed in the Maghreb, pushed North Africans deeper into the desert until they had little choice but to become trans-Saharan traders. Mobility, here, was as much pressure as opportunity. In northern Mali, she visits al-Khalil in 2009 and finds its trade booming. The oldest permanent house there dates from 1993 and began as a store for arms for the separatist rebellion of the early 1990s. Commerce, rebellion and settlement, in the Sahara, are often built with the same walls. What these cases share is a desert that is never empty. It is inhabited not by permanent settlements alone but by routes, encounters, negotiations, and obligations.

Scheele applies the same method to the subjects that dominate the headlines. Slavery, racism, religious militancy, terrorism and desertification each get their own treatment, and in each case, as a 

reviewer for

 

Foreign Affairs

 

notes

, she shows how familiar narratives often grow out of outsiders’ fantasies of the desert as an inhospitable, impermeable barrier. She does not romanticize that circulation. The same routes carried enslaved people, reproduced racial hierarchies and concentrated wealth in few hands. Nor did colonial rule invent every division: Saharan societies had their own rivalries and territorial distinctions. But colonial administrations hardened them into borders drawn around distant capitals, and began to treat older routes as marginal, illicit, or dangerous. Independent states inherited that architecture, and with it a contradiction: communities keep depending on cross-border movement, while official policy reads that movement as a failure of control.

This is why emptiness is never an innocent description. Calling an inhabited space empty lets existing relationships be ignored and makes outside intervention look like the first arrival of order, development or connectivity. Once a territory is imagined as a void, the people who live there are easily treated as obstacles to somebody else’s project.

That contradiction is not a historical footnote; it is what the current diplomacy is fought over. Tin Zaouatine is a border town that both capitals see as a security problem. 

ADF Magazine

 

reports

 that Algeria fears fighting between Mali’s army and Tuareg rebels could spread to Algeria’s own Tuareg population. For the people who live there, kinship, trade and pasture run across a line that governments treat as the front of a dispute. Scheele’s history makes visible what the security language hides: that the border cuts through communities, rather than between them.

The same tension runs through the Alliance of Sahel States. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger left the Economic Community of West African States in 2025 in the name of sovereignty, and their ministers have discussed 

harmonized travel and identity documents

 to ease movement among their own citizens. Yet, as the Migration Policy Institute observes, their exit 

exposed a tension between regional free-movement commitments and tightening security controls

. Mobility is being re-sorted by membership: it is a right for some and suspicious for everyone else.

Niger shows how fast the rules can turn. In November 2023, its military government repealed a 2015 law that had criminalized the transport of migrants. By April 2025, it was warning, 

according to AFP

, that mass arrivals of non-Nigerien migrants expelled from Algeria could upset the country’s security balance. The same movement is a trade, a crime, or a threat, depending on who is moving, in which direction, and which capital is speaking.

Policy built on the same imagination misses what keeps people alive. Security strategies aim to close routes without asking what work, exchange, and mutual dependence those routes sustain. Development programs talk of integrating peripheral regions that have long been integrated into networks that do not follow national maps. And the cost of getting it wrong falls on the people with the least power to contest it: those left at Point Zéro, who must walk through the desert to Assamaka, with some reportedly dying along the way, according to 

UNHCR, IOM and the Mixed Migration Centre

.

Scheele’s book resolves none of this. But it changes what counts as normal. If circulation has been the Sahara’s ordinary condition for centuries, then drivers, traders, pastoralists, and migrants are not anomalies to be managed; they are the region’s own infrastructure. The question for the people in and around the desert is not what Europe should learn from the past. It is who decides which crossings count as trade, which as trafficking, and which as a threat; and who ends up at Point Zéro when the answer changes.

author: Nathaniel Njeru Mugo
title: The names on the ice
content:
Mount Kenya’s glaciers carry names such as Lewis, Gregory, Tyndall, Darwin, Forel and Heim. Within a few years, the ice carrying those names may be gone. Two of the less famous glaciers, Cesar and Josef, tell the story better.

In 1899, Halford Mackinder set out to make the 

first recorded ascent of Batian

 with six Europeans, 66 Swahilis, two Maasai guides and 96 Kikuyu. Among the Europeans were César Ollier and Joseph Brocherel, Alpine guides from Courmayeur in Italy. Brocherel was also listed as a porter. Both men left their names on the mountain: 

Cesar Glacier and Josef Glacier

.

The 96 Kikuyu did not.

That discrepancy invites an easy story about Europeans overwriting an African map. The mountain is less tidy. Lower down, African names persist: 

Kikami

, 

from the Kikuyu word for hyrax;

 

Mbairunyi

, 

“Place of Fighting”;

 

Gacheno

, 

“Place of Danger”;

 

Kethimbui

, 

“Place of Rest.”

 They record animals, conflict, fear and respite rather than distant scientists and explorers. The pattern is not absence but altitude. The higher the map goes, the whiter it gets.

Even the summit area complicates that pattern. 

Mackinder adopted Batian, Nelion and Lenana, names of Maasai figures, on the suggestion of Sidney Langford Hinde

, a British colonial officer in Maasailand. Africans appear throughout the mountain’s nomenclature — as guides and porters, as informants and sources of names. Europeans were usually the people deciding which names entered the map, and which endured.

At the ice line, the contrast becomes harder to miss. Lewis is named for a geologist; Darwin for Charles Darwin. The ice became an index of European science, honoring men with no particular connection to Mount Kenya. Tyndall is the sharpest case. 

His experiments established that gases including carbon dioxide and water vapor absorb radiant heat

. The glacier bearing his name is disappearing in a changing climate.

There is a second imbalance. The industrialized countries from which many of those explorers and scientists came account for a disproportionate share of the emissions changing the planet’s climate. From 1850 to 2019, 

the IPCC calculates

, developed countries produced 57% of cumulative fossil fuel and industrial carbon dioxide emissions; Africa, just 3%. The names were assigned here; most of the carbon was emitted elsewhere.

Nor was every European name an act of personal vanity. When J.W. Gregory surveyed Mount Kenya, 

he named glaciers after Forel and Heim for a practical reason: glaciers needed names if they were to be described and mapped

.

Useful to whom is a small question, but not an empty one.

The 

Mountain Club of Kenya’s guide

 records that in 1924 porters insisted they had seen a lion beside a tarn; Melhuish and Dutton called it Simba Tarn. The porters’ observation survived on the map; their names did not. The same men named another tarn after Gitchini, Melhuish’s personal servant, who accompanied him on mountain journeys.

Another name connects Mount Kenya with Kilimanjaro. The missionary 

Johannes Rebmann joined Johann Ludwig Krapf in Mombasa in 1846

. In 1848, Rebmann reported snow on Kilimanjaro. On 

December 3, 1849, Krapf sighted Mount Kenya

, whose name he recorded as Kenia or Kegnia after hearing it from Kamba people. The precise etymology is disputed, but an African name entered the European written record and eventually named the country.

Krapf got a glacier too.

There is precedent for reconsidering what mountains record. At 

Tanganyika’s independence in 1961, Kilimanjaro’s Kaiser-Wilhelm-Spitze became Uhuru Peak

. The summit proclaimed freedom; the ice retained a different history. 

Rebmann Glacier

 was not renamed. Kenya became independent two years later, and Krapf Glacier kept its name too.

In 1963, 

twelve of Mount Kenya’s named glaciers still survived

: Northey, Krapf, Gregory, Lewis, Melhuish, Diamond, Darwin, Forel, Heim, Tyndall, Cesar and Josef. Their names did not change. Kenya nonetheless 

renamed Lake Rudolf as Lake Turkana in 1975

. The machinery existed. It simply never reached the ice.

Lewis Glacier 

lost 90 % of its volume between 1934 and 2010

. 

Prinz and colleagues found

 Lewis Glacier’s mass balance most sensitive to atmospheric moisture, through snowfall, cloud cover, and surface reflectivity. Their model showed that increased snow accumulation could produce net gains in ice without significant cooling. Satellite mapping from 2021 and 2022 found just 

0.069 square kilometres of glacier ice left on Mount Kenya

, about 4.2% of its area around 1900. The 

World Meteorological Organization

 projects that the glaciers 

could disappear by 2030

. The exact year may shift. The direction does not.

Would renaming a disappearing glacier be vanity? Not if it changed who gets to decide what the map remembers. It would not save the ice, and changing the labels by decree while excluding the communities whose knowledge shaped the mountain would repeat the old method. The names we retain are choices about whose contributions deserve to be remembered.

And then there is Gitchini. Melhuish had two names on the mountain, a point and a glacier. The 

glacier had disappeared by 1987

; he still has the point. Gitchini had one. The tarn is still there, but it is now called Hanging Tarn.

The glaciers are doing the reverse: the ice is disappearing, and the names are staying.

author: Tsogo Kupa
title: The country that never grieved
content:
It is said that the best films are those that truly begin only once they’re over. When the film’s images are embedded in your memory, its noises echo in your ears, and its themes steep in your thoughts. This is not to say the viewing experience itself isn’t transformative, but when films reach for something higher than distraction and pure entertainment, they offer something you take home with you, a meditation. 

Advik Beni’s feature debut, 

Mother, you have not died yet. But you will. And when you do, you will finally be alive again

, is one of those meditations, and it’s rooted in mourning: for a mother, a country, a city, and an identity. It’s teeming with texture, pictured in warm, cotton-pulpy celluloid, and elevated by a sound design that balances the granular and mosaic. It blurs the lines between fact and fiction, and while there are moments that too obviously remind you that you’re not watching a documentary, its grounding in the factual gives the film a unique brilliance.

The film’s simple plot, of a middle-aged woman in Cato Manor taking care of her ailing mother, betrays the contours of memory, culture, family, and history the film traverses. 

Mother, you have not died

 

yet

 is an experimental documentary that makes the political personal. Similar to Milisuthando Bongela’s acclaimed self-titled film, it rummages through personal and family archives to explore the sinews of what South Africa means to South Africans in the many iterations of what it has been. It centers its personal and historical inquiry around the reverberating question of what it means to be Indian in post-apartheid South Africa. 

It’s not the first film to explore South African Indian identity, but it’s the first I’ve seen that attempts to reconcile the beauty, grief, and conflicts that form part of Indian identity in South Africa. The country’s first Indians came as indentured laborers in the 19th century to service the growing sugar plantations in KwaZulu-Natal. The ethno-national group wove its own identity into the tapestry of South Africa’s growing industrialized cultural landscape; yet its relationship with Black South Africans has been tumultuous. Many of these frictions and wounds merge in Cato Manor, a neighborhood in the port city of Durban originally inhabited by former Indian indentured laborers. Appropriately, Cato Manor is where 

Mother, you have not died

 yet, takes place. The city bears the weight of historical racial violence between Blacks and Indians, and the preservation and decay of its first inhabitants’ heritage. 

I talked to the writer & director of the film, Advik Beni, a South African filmmaker, programmer, and teacher based in Los Angeles. In the interview, we try to peel back the layers of their ambitious feature debut and put its kaleidoscope of ideas into focus. 

Mother, you have not died yet

 had its world premiere at the FID Marseille film festival this year, where it won the Audience Award and recently celebrated its North American debut at the Camden International Film Festival.

Tsogo Kupa

I can see overtures between your work and Milisuthando Bongela’s. Why do you think this experimental and auto-ethnographic form of storytelling has been useful when trying to navigate what it means to live in a post-apartheid South Africa?

Advik Beni

It’s like at the forefront of every work I make. So our industry is so new, but we find a lot of the films falling into a sort of European, Western model of filmmaking. And it’s not just a South African issue. A lot of countries that have gone through this history of colonialism adapt to that Western model of storytelling. But for me, one of the beautiful things about being South African is our type of storytelling, our oral traditions. And this goes cross-culturally. So that’s something I always try to adapt into cinema, which is like an impossible task. As soon as you write or record orality, it’s not orality anymore. It loses the beauty of it, which is that mutability, that ability to change and adapt and go in with humor, or pull away the humor from an audience. You can’t really do that in cinema. But I think it’s something, as South African filmmakers, we should be trying to do, which is to find our own language and our own form of filmmaking. And for me, it’s fallen between this world of experimental essay, ethnographic, and the personal, because I think, like all countries, but more so in South Africa, the personal is inseparable from the political. I think we should be trying to read, rethink, and question: why are we making a film that looks like a French film or like an American film? Why do our stories need to live in those vessels? Like, why don’t we try to build our own vessels that are more true to our own upbringing and surroundings?

Tsogo Kupa

There’s a heavy use of archive in your film, and one of the concerns that the main character in the film continuously brings up is the idea of losing heritage, losing a language. So, oral storytelling takes huge prominence in the film, as does the role of the archive. How did you approach not only making your adaptation of archive in a very textile and deconstructive way, but how did you take on the responsibility of creating your own archive? 

Advik Beni

I’ve always felt this dichotomy, and this is completely false, and it’s just in my mind, but there are those who really want to preserve the archive. And these are, a lot of times, institutions. And there are those who completely want to burn the archive. And this is not a binary that actually exists, but it’s the way my mind works. I try to find the in-between space. And I stand between both schools; I understand the beauty in holding on to history, but it’s who has the power, who’s holding on to this history, and whose history. And I can speak as a South African Indian that our archives are not held in those institutions in any sort of tangible way. It’s held in the recipes being passed down, in the photo album of your loved ones, and in people pointing out and telling stories. Like those moments hold our archives. So for me, this film was trying to play with that concept; it was taking those official archives, for example, the 1949 riot image, and creating this kind of bricolage collage effect by putting these other archives, which I think are just as important, these oral histories, these thoughts, these imaginaries. Because we often don’t have the resources to properly archive. How do we incorporate what we believe and our thoughts and our histories alongside that which is more stringent? For example, getting an image from Getty Archives, that exists in these structures that say: “yes, this is real”, but ours don’t exist in the structures that say: “yes, this is real.” Outside of us putting it forward and saying, “No, it’s real.”

Tsogo Kupa

One of the interesting things about archive, especially in the way that you described it, and how it also appears in your film, is navigating this idea of the gaze. As African filmmakers, you’re constantly wrestling with the colonial gaze. In this film, gaze manifests itself in different ways. How do you confront your own gaze in the film?

Advik Beni

I mean, the protagonist is my auntie. So we have a very close relationship, and the film kind of was built upon a conversation about the country. It was never a film at first. It was just a discussion on how to explain South Africa to anyone outside of its borders. But then became something wholly different when my aunt’s mother passed away. And then this idea of reenactment entered, and it was just a kind of experiment. Like, I try to adopt a model of filmmaking that focuses more on the process than the product. And that’s complicated because the product needs to be something. After all, in this world that we live in, of capitalism and whatnot, you need a good product to start your next process. But for me, putting that emphasis on process, putting that emphasis on the process that is not hierarchical, that is hybridized, that allows an exchange between everyone on the project. I think where gaze tends to be problematic is when you’re pasting something onto a subject, or you’re painting something onto a character. But if there’s exchange, if there’s dialogue in that process, if they are authors of it as well as you. I think it’s really important because you want the community to be in conversation with the piece whilst you’re making the piece, not just once you make it and put it out there. There was a spine to the film written in a sort of treatment form, but it was all about those people who were enacting and reenacting parts of the film to give what they wanted and to block out what they didn’t want.

Tsogo Kupa

I think there’s a very interesting way in which all the different aspects of filmmaking speak to each other. It’s a film that you feel like you can touch, that it’s moving, hypnotic, slow, and transcendental. What is the intentionality behind making a film that’s so sensorially rich, and the relationship with your team to achieve that?

Advik Beni

 I came to LA for the California Institute of the Arts, and the reason I came here is that they teach you how to make film on celluloid. So I’ve always been used to using my hands and using the physical medium to tell a story. My producer and animator of this film (Nehal Vyas) is incredible at stop motion, and we worked together on how to bring those archives to life in a new form, bringing them back, making them a part of the image. So for me, that’s one part of it. It’s just my love for that kind of tactile experience. It was important for me to shoot this film on Super 8 and 16. And even though travelling from South Africa to LA to process the film was scary, it was something really important because that medium, the physical medium itself, it’s not designed for black and brown skin. It was literally made with test subjects, which were white people. So the exposure and the physical chemistry of the film are designed to have proper exposure for white skin. So that act of just trying to shoot my own landscape, my own people, the people around me, felt like a sort of very small rebellion. My people never had the privilege to own film at that time because Kodak boycotted South Africa, so there was no access except for the white oppressors to come from places like the UK to shoot our skin. I mean, now I have access. Let me use that same medium that we didn’t have access to in the ‘70s, ‘80s, ‘60s and shoot people and places which were never shot on that medium.

Tsogo Kupa

And the sound design?

Advik Beni

I think a big part was before shooting; I wanted to record with five mics. Like, did we use all five mics? Absolutely not. But you’re getting audio from both left and right, pointed at different angles of the room. You’re getting different kinds of surroundings that aren’t necessarily in the scene. I think it’s very important to me to capture the sort of spatiality of Cato Manor, because it’s a place I used to go constantly growing up, because that’s where my granddad lived and my auntie lived, and she always cooked for us. The memory that’s triggered whenever I go there is just the sounds. It’s everywhere. It’s within the kitchen. But you also hear the dog from next door; you’re hearing somebody skating down the road; you’re hearing a taxi go past with music. All of that sound is constant. Then I think in the more experimental essay section with the voiceover, it was just capturing this liminal space, because for me, that space is sort of an ancestral realm in many ways, a space where the mother is alive and dead and she’s speaking to the mother, her actual mother, but also the reenacted mother. So for me, it was just capturing that liminality through sound, that between us, nothing’s quite settled. But her voice is settled, but the surroundings are not quite settled.

Tsogo Kupa

I’m interested in the use of repetition in the film. What’s the motivation behind the use of routines and repetition throughout the film?

Advik Beni

I would see the same act of gardening and cooking, and that was just something I admired so much. But I think another part of it, which looks at the bigger picture, is that the film itself is about cyclicality and repetition. It’s about that final sequence; without giving too much away, it looks at that 1949 riot and it looks at the 2021 riots, and that’s not shocking because we know that tensions were there, but that cyclicality is disheartening. So, conceptually and structurally, that’s when I started to understand that South Africa is a country that didn’t properly grieve for the end of apartheid. We kind of put a plaster over a bleeding wound and hoped for the best. And I think what we’re seeing, like 30 years afterwards, is these wounds slowly starting to open again. So for me, that cycle is happening. That’s all we can, as South Africans, hope for. That we can find a place where we can just actually create tangible repair and tangible shift. I think a lot of people have to survive in some way, and our routines help us to give us something. “Oh, I’m going to wake up today. I’m going to do the gardening. I’m going to cut the wood. I’m going to do my prayer.” You know, it gives you a sense of knowing, even if the larger world around you is unknowing.

Tsogo Kupa

In my experience with the film, there are three acts of grieving. So you have the grieving of Durban before the 1949 riots, where there was some semblance of unity between Blacks and Indians before the riots. There’s also a grief of the solidarity between Black and Indian South Africans in the late ‘70s and ‘80s. There’s also a broader grief around Durban as a city. So how do you feel like your film also grieves with Durban as a location as well? Because Durban feels like a location, but is also its own character in the film.

Advik Beni

It’s my city. But as you said, it’s so complicated because it also has the highest concentration of Indian people. And that relationship to Black people is so tenuous, and it’s been up and down over the years, and thinking through the history of a place like Cato Manner, which was so pivotal in the fight against apartheid. So it’s embedded in the film, through that archive of the riots and the barbershop, which is a barbershop that has been in my family for 70 years. Still in Durban, there’s a lack of integration in a way that’s really harmful in the long run. And it’s something I noticed within my own community is just sort of, why is it that my population, my people, are trying to take this hierarchical approach? And yes, it has to do with the system, has to do with the lack of care from the city. It’s also the lack of infrastructure. Those feed into each other; they’re inseparable. It creates those tensions. And with the 2021 riots, we saw that too. But then there were so many things layered on top of that. It was that lack of infrastructure, the tiredness of people who have been disgruntled for so long because they’re being pushed down. And of course it’s going to come out in ways that are not fun and not beautiful, like it’s going to come out in ways that are harmful to people. And that’s completely inseparable.

Tsogo Kupa

As someone who works between two countries, how do you reconcile making cinema that is very rooted, genuine, and offers insight to South African audiences while also being accessible to a global audience?

Advik Beni

Whether this was truly accessible to a global audience, I think, is a question we’ll still figure out as it shows more, because I do think it’s very specific to South Africa to delve into Cato Manor; it’s very specific. But I think this idea of sort of tensions between two communities that were both subjugated, yes, at different levels. It’s something that rings true throughout; even here in LA, you see, see these kinds of tensions occurring. So for me, that’s the thing that makes it sort of universal. It’s not something South African-specific, but much more heightened in South Africa because of its history. So it’s a battle. It’s something that I will stand strong on, though. We’ve got to find our own language. We’ve got to find our own places. The festival system is something that’s not completely beneficial for filmmakers. It’s beneficial for the festival. So it’s also like a give-and-take; we know why we want to be in those festivals. It’s like there’s a weird balance and a weird tension there as well. But I think as filmmakers, we’ve got to just believe in, as cheesy as it is, our own stories. I think more importantly for us as South Africans is, like, how do we want to tell the story? We don’t want to be fetishised. We don’t want to be looked at as this kind of other. We want to be telling it our way for our people. And if you resonate with that, cool. But it’s for us. It’s for us to figure out because we’ve got things to figure out. We’ve got lots of things to figure out, and we should be doing it now.

author: Laura Burocco
title: How Lula’s army beat the algorithm
content:
The outcome of recent elections in Brazil carries exceptional political and moral significance. In the runoff on October 25, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term with about 52 percent of the vote, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. It was a geopolitical victory not only for South America, but for the entire world — offering hope that it is still possible to free ourselves from the far-right extremist wave. In the contest between Latin America — “Prospero’s mirror,” as Richard Morse called it in his 1988 book 

O Espelho de Próspero

 — and Prospero himself, the United States, the main political victory in South America has come from the left.

Daron Acemoglu, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and author of 

What Happened to Liberal Democracy

?, argues that Brazil’s 2026 presidential elections are the most important elections outside the US. In an 

interview

 with BBC Brasil, he states that “much of the enormous concentration of economic power we see in the United States has been driven by technology companies that control information.” According to Acemoglu, the alternative could be “a liberalism that serves workers, based on shared prosperity, public services and democratic participation, drawing on the experience of Brazil’s first Workers’ Party (PT) governments in the early 2000s, which gained international visibility through their social policies and the active role of the state.” Perhaps, by returning to his roots, Lula can not only fulfill his often-repeated promise to “make the best government in the history of Brazil” during this final term, but also strengthen the increasingly influential role of the South in building an alternative international order.

Tensions between Washington and Brussels could strengthen Brazil’s position as a political alternative to North American pressure, especially given Lula’s interest in international mediation, most recently in Ukraine, and Europe’s increasingly right-wing shift under Ursula von der Leyen.

In a region where only Brazil and Uruguay are not governed by the right, and given the strained relations with the US, Brazil will need to strengthen its integration with the BRICS countries, particularly by consolidating relations with China and, indirectly, Russia, thereby strengthening its role on the international stage and promoting a more multipolar world order. According to journalist 

Jamil Chade

, for the first time since the 1964 coup that established the military dictatorship, Brazil has become the center of “the largest foreign offensive in its recent history.” Washington considers the country strategically important for consolidating its hegemony in South America, containing Chinese expansion, and gaining access to resources, particularly rare earth minerals. Limiting the independence of Brazilian foreign policy has therefore become a priority for the US. Aggressive US policy and practice against the sovereignty of other nations has found further room to expand through the unlimited freedom and impunity with which major high-tech multinationals operate (see this 

research

 by Sleeping Giants Brasil).

Lula’s victory did not come on a level playing field. Following a complaint from Lula’s campaign, which alleged that Meta repeatedly reduced the visibility of his posts while promoting content from his opponent, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) asked the company to explain itself. Meta attributed its conduct to “technical problems.” The interference affected not only the campaign but also 

independent media outlets

. The National Forum for the Democratization of Communication subsequently launched the campaign 

Meta, Não se Meta

 (“Meta, Don’t Interfere”) and organized a series of demonstrations, while a group of 

13 US lawmakers sent a letter to Mark Zuckerberg

 requesting clarification regarding the allegations of unequal treatment. The 

TSE eventually ruled in Lula’s favor

, ordering Meta to “ensure its artificial intelligence tool applies identical criteria to both candidates.”

Politics is now conducted through posts, Instagram videos and online comments on networks controlled — or, if you prefer, moderated — by the high-tech companies at the top of the global economy. All are aligned with the political establishment. Brazil’s 2018 elections illustrated this dynamic: the UFBA researcher 

Tatiana Dourado

 documented 346 false stories circulated during the campaign, exposing how social networks, particularly through the dissemination of information via WhatsApp, enable digital manipulation and allow tech companies to influence elections in any democracy. In 2022, Brazil was once again at risk. But perhaps memories of the deaths caused by the government’s public-health policies during the pandemic, and of the country’s international isolation, ultimately prevailed. This year’s election period saw record allegations of interference: funding from the US; interference by Meta and the TSE; pressure from right-wing businesses such as Zona Sul, a supermarket chain that urged employees to “vote consciously” to change Brazil, implicitly backing the anti-PT candidate; false WhatsApp claims that voters’ individual taxpayer numbers (CPFs) had been blocked; and, on election day itself, the obstruction of public transport, allegedly orchestrated by high-ranking figures in the country’s federal and state politics.

Lula’s army

In response to the results of the first round and the reported levels of interference and obstruction, the 

Exército do Lula

 (Lula’s Army), led by André Janones, a federal deputy from the 

Rede Sustentabilidade

 party and a strategic ally of the PT, employed the same tactics as the evangelical pastors backing the candidacy of what Lula’s supporters call the “militia clan” — a reference to the Bolsonaro family and its alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro’s paramilitary militias. Its weapon was delirium. Janones engaged on digital turf, creating a WhatsApp channel that directed the masses online, instructing them to copy, paste and post his content — videos, hashtags, Google searches — followed by the command: “Make it explode!” During the final week of Lula’s second-round campaign, the channel boasted nearly 11 million active followers.

According to 

Felipe Pena

, a political commentator and journalism lecturer in the Department of Social Communication at the Federal Fluminense University (UFF), Janones’s achievement lay in his understanding of digital natives — those born with access to the internet — and his ability to identify the right format, language and communication strategies for reaching this electorate. In the days leading up to the election, Instagram, X, TikTok and Facebook feeds were flooded with images of people making the letter L for Lula while wearing the colors of the Brazilian flag. The gesture went viral thanks to coordinated actions by Lula’s Army, joined by many celebrities. Janones organized what was described as “the largest livestream in Brazilian political history,” with 21.69 million views, a peak of 773,400 simultaneous viewers, an average of 403,700 viewers, more than 174 million chat reactions and 13.46 million messages. A mixture of anxiety and adrenaline became increasingly palpable through the compulsive reproduction of WhatsApp messages and the ever-faster sharing of content across social media. The goal was to “drive the algorithm crazy,” and it likely succeeded. Though the PT campaign initially kept its distance from the channel, Janones was soon fully integrated into the president’s campaign team. Following Lula’s victory, the PT expressed its desire to invite the deputy to join the party and to give him a position in the president’s fourth term. Lula also linked the election result to the way he intends to conduct his next term. He has promised to expand popular participation in decision-making and stated that “digital communication will gain considerable ground.” Janones is expected to do the same. Some have already identified him as a potential presidential candidate in 2030, a possibility he himself 

has not ruled out

. If the PT has failed over the years to create a successor to Lula, Janones appears to have created the opportunity for himself.

The Janones phenomenon has also taken hold of imaginations beyond Brazil, with invitations from Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum and Peronist leaders in Argentina.

Detachment from reality

Janones’s media campaign took off following the second debate between the two presidential candidates. Both debates were a horrifying spectacle. During the first, Bolsonaro spent the evening hovering behind Lula, imitating Trump’s propaganda strategies, and displaying the word “corrupt” on the palm of his hand. Lula initially tried to maintain a minimum level of decency, but eventually had to descend to his opponent’s abysmal level, because this now seems to be the only way to reach voters. The second debate reached one of its lowest points when Flávio Bolsonaro called Lula “nine fingers,” prompting the incumbent president to explicitly accuse him of being a militia member.

A petition calling for fact-checking during TV Globo’s broadcast of the presidential debate, which gathered more than one million signatures, was, unsurprisingly, rejected by the network. According to the results published by the website 

Checagem ao Vivo

, 63 statements by Lula and 103 by Bolsonaro were analyzed. Of the statements made by Lula, 58 were classified as factual and five as “not quite accurate.” In Bolsonaro’s case, eight statements were deemed factual, 54 false, 37 inaccurate, and the rest inconclusive. Even 

Folha de S.Paulo

, traditionally critical of the president, had to acknowledge Lula’s superiority in his confrontation with Flávio Bolsonaro.

The disconnection from reality underpinning the PL’s campaign was such that, in São Paulo, people gathered in support of Bolsonaro carrying an inflatable missile and calling on the US to bomb Brazil. These same people describe themselves as fervent patriots. Patriots like their candidate, who, following a decision by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes requiring him to surrender his passports to the Federal Police in Brasília within 24 hours, fled to Argentina after the deadline expired, before traveling on to the US. Just as his father had done, the defeated Flávio Bolsonaro refused to accept Lula’s victory, even though the declaration came from his own ally Nunes Marques, president of the TSE. While Flávio Bolsonaro was being ridiculed around the world, Senator Sergio Moro, the judge who ordered Lula’s arrest and is affiliated with the PL, 

declared

 that “Brazil is not experiencing institutional normality and, therefore, Flávio’s departure from the country is understandable.”

A flagrant coup attempt

There is no doubt that what unfolded live on the night of Brazil’s last presidential election was criminal, amounting to a violation of both the constitutional principle of judicial impartiality, in the case of the Superior Electoral Court, and the right to vote, in the case of the private companies and political representatives behind the transport shortages. It also amounts to a brazen attempt at a coup d’état. Nunes Marques, president of the TSE, the person who should guarantee respect for the constitutional voting rights of Brazilian citizens, openly demonstrated that he favored the son of the man who had appointed him to the court he currently heads.

Beginning on Saturday, Brazil’s two largest low-cost airlines, Gol and Azul, as well as LATAM, canceled flights, citing maintenance requirements and technical problems. Most were bound for the Northeast, Lula’s region of origin and, historically, the PT’s main electoral stronghold. A similar situation occurred in Bahia, where Salvador’s mayor, a Bolsonaro ally, ordered 75 buses to remain in their depots. According to 

Folha de S.Paulo

, he blamed union members who allegedly wanted to place PT stickers on bus windows. Following a complaint by the Brazil of Hope Federation, a PT-led coalition, the Regional Electoral Court of Bahia ordered the immediate restoration of the entire fleet and issued an arrest warrant for the city’s mobility secretary. A similar shortage affected São Paulo, where Mayor Ricardo Nunes was accused of reducing the bus fleet and increasing road checks. According to the PT’s state president, only 60 percent of buses were operating; the party sought the arrest of the municipal secretary for urban mobility and transport, Celso Jorge Caldeira, for failing to comply with the TRE-SP ruling requiring the entire fleet to operate free of charge.

For this reason, with the agreement of both candidates — a position the losing candidate later sought to deny — a request was submitted to the TSE to extend voting hours in the states of São Paulo and Bahia. It was accepted by Supreme Federal Court Justice Cristiano Zanin, despite the TSE president’s attempt to delay the decision. Anyone who arrived at their polling station before its scheduled closing time was guaranteed the right to vote. The problem was that many polling stations had been relocated without prior notice. According to CNN Brasil, the TSE recorded changes at more than 400 polling stations. Similar abuses were recorded in the Brazilian Amazon, where the obligation to provide transportation for voters in rural areas is particularly significant: people often have to travel for hours, sometimes even days, to reach their polling stations. Against this backdrop, the former minister for Indigenous peoples, Sonia Guajajara, denounced the Superior Electoral Court’s refusal to grant general authorization to the National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples, the Special Secretariat for Indigenous Health and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples to use their facilities to ensure transportation for Indigenous voters. President Lula also called for the arrest of mayors responsible for electoral offenses arising from the obstruction of voter transport, describing the situation as “abominable.” Authorities are proceeding with the removal of mayors involved in the transport disruptions and reporting the responsible private companies.

Online and in the streets

Despite all the criminal actions that characterized the second round in particular, Brazil managed to accomplish a historic feat by re-electing Lula for a fourth and final presidential term. But if social networks, thanks to Lula’s Army, managed to counter Meta’s unfavorable algorithm, the success must be attributed to an explosive combination of networks online and in the streets. On one side, an army on the internet; on the other, a mass mobilization in which millions of voters who had abstained in the first round returned to the polls. It was an extraordinary team effort involving media and generations, the internet and street demonstrations, older people — including the president himself, who is 81 — and young people, who made a significant contribution to these elections.

Following the first-round defeat, 2,000 students from the Federal Fluminense University in Rio de Janeiro took to the streets of Niterói. The following day, students from the Federal University of Pernambuco in Recife joined them, followed by students in at least 13 states and the Federal District by October 7. In 1992, the National Union of Students brought thousands of students into the streets with their faces painted in the colors of the Brazilian flag to demand that Congress impeach President Fernando Collor de Mello and to protest against corruption. The 

caras pintadas

 (painted faces) returned to the streets in 2026 with the 

Estudantes com Lula

 (“Students with Lula”) campaign, declaring that “democratic confrontation is in the DNA of Brazilian students.” Like all mobilizations, the campaign aimed to convince undecided voters. Older people across the country were accompanied by relatives and friends, enabling them to cast their votes in support of democracy and against dictatorship, convinced that every single vote counts. Many images of older voters showed people originally from the Northeast, like Lula himself, reflecting a longstanding alliance with the president and with a homeland repeatedly insulted by both Bolsonaro father and son. Young people represented, in part, workers angered by the labor reform package proposed by Bolsonaro, and students who had benefited from state-supported education initiatives — including ProUni, 

Pé-de-Meia

 and the quota systems for university recruitment — introduced during Lula’s administrations.

Against all the attacks on public transport, in a demonstration of the motto “Brazilians never give up,” mutual-aid groups emerged to provide lifts and alternative transport, both within cities and between states, circulating useful information from one end of the country to the other through videos, posts and audio messages. One noteworthy initiative was the discreet mobilization of people working with Indigenous communities. Through solidarity networks, they organized fundraising several days in advance to ensure that the constitutional right of Indigenous Brazilians to vote would be respected if the responsible public authorities arrived late or failed to intervene. Any attempt to deny Indigenous peoples access to this right is particularly serious, as it reinforces the intentions expressed by Jair Bolsonaro during his 2019–2022 presidency to revive the dictatorship’s assimilationist policies, which sought to erase Indigenous peoples as distinct ethnic groups and integrate them into wider society as ordinary workers and citizens.

Another important factor in the victory was the breadth of alliances formed between the cultural and political spheres — a massive stand in favor of Lula among prominent figures in cinema, music and the arts. One of the most notable political alliances was with Erika Hilton, a Black transgender socialist who became the most-voted congresswoman in Brazilian history and a driving force behind the constitutional amendment abolishing the six-day working week. This historic victory for Brazil’s working class — and Bolsonaro’s opposition to it — increased voter turnout in Lula’s favor. Similarly, the alliance between right and left, exemplified by Vice-President Alckmin, Lula’s longtime rival, highlights the distinction between political opponents and incompetent, fanatical and criminal adversaries.

Violence in the wake of defeat

Violence spread throughout the election campaign and continued in the days following the vote, prompting lawyer Marco Aurélio Carvalho, coordinator of Lula’s electoral campaign, to denounce the escalation of political violence linked to the far right.

Four Lula voters were killed by Bolsonaro supporters. According to a report published by 

CartaCapital

, Ewerton Rodrigues da Silva, 34, was shot three times following an argument provoked by Bolsonaro supporters. Anderson Pires Bolandin, 35, collapsed after being shot next to a fuel pump and died in the ambulance; Sebastião Dusso Braga Neto, 34, was shot in the abdomen and died of his injuries despite receiving medical treatment. Environmental engineer Marcelo de Oliveira Rocha, 30, was declared brain-dead after being brutally beaten in the early hours of Saturday, October 24. City councilor Iara Pimentel (PT) was targeted in a planned attack during a motorcade on Saturday night. Maria das Neves Filha, president of the Federal District branch of the Brazilian Women’s Union, and Edilamar Melo, president of the Gama Youth Association, were violently attacked by a retired military police officer. 

Paolla Paullyne Freitas Araújo de Alencar Vital

, a trans woman and former city council candidate in Alagoas, was shot and killed, and 

Elisabete Martins Chaves

 died after being hit by a car. Numerous other cases of non-fatal violence were also recorded.

While people celebrated Lula’s victory, 

APIB

 — 

the Articulation of Indigenous Peoples of Brazil

 — and numerous Indigenous associations reported cases of murder and violence against their communities following Bolsonaro’s defeat. The Ministries of Indigenous Peoples, of Human Rights and Citizenship, and of Racial Equality are working together to request investigations into reports of violence against Indigenous peoples, 

quilombola

 communities and Afro-Brazilian religious communities. The minister of Indigenous peoples, Eloy Terena, a member of the Terena people, reported 

on social media

 that he had contacted the Federal Police to investigate allegations of deaths and violations against Indigenous populations in Mato Grosso do Sul, where Indigenous leaders reported murders and threats to poison water sources used by their communities. The Federal Prosecutor’s Office gave the 

municipality of Tacuru

 48 hours to clarify the poisoning threats. In the same region, the home of 90-year-old Guaraní and Kaiowá spiritual leader Roberta Ximenes, known as 

Ñandesy

 Roberta, was set 

on fire

, destroying sacred objects used in traditional rituals.

No less violent are the manifestations of structural racism — the legacy of the country’s history of colonization and slavery — which persist in Brazilian society regardless of the election outcome, perpetuated by the growing political influence of the Bolsonaro militia clan and its allies in government. During a Bolsonaro support event, a Black man was seen being walked on a leash by a man dressed in yellow and green. As reported in 

O Globo

, the man denied that the act was racist and justified it as a form of “satire,” concluding: “If I offended any Brazilian, that was not my intention.” The newspaper itself referred to the white man by his full name, while identifying the man who had been brought there in chains simply as “the Black man.”

The reaction of the business class to the election outcome confirmed how deeply intertwined race and class assumptions are. 

CartaCapital

 reported that Lula’s victory caused Brazil’s financial markets to open the week in decline, triggering the automatic trading-halt mechanism three minutes after the opening — a mechanism that had not been activated since the beginning of the pandemic in March 2020. The backlash was not limited to the stock market. The day after the election, cases were reported of transport companies dismissing employees who had supported President Lula’s re-election. On the same day, a large ice-cream chain in the interior of São Paulo state announced on social media that it would no longer provide food assistance or make donations because it was “tired” of helping people who preferred to “live off state assistance.” In response, the Ministry of Labor and Employment announced it would investigate reports of threats of dismissal, harassment and other forms of electoral coercion targeting workers who supported Lula.

The future of political participation

One particularly striking 

comment

 from one of the “recruited” by Lula’s Army was an observation about how Bolsonaro supporters must feel when they are indoctrinated around the clock by their extremist conservative leaders, often evangelical pastors: “It has only been three weeks since we joined the WhatsApp groups, sharing, commenting, liking posts, and we are already feeling unwell. Now imagine this being the daily routine of a Bolsonaro supporter. They spend all day doing this. No wonder these people end up in psychosis, drinking detergent and praying to ET.” He refers to the ANVISA case: after the agency suspended batches of Ypê detergent over bacterial-contamination risks, Bolsonaro supporters accused it of political persecution, with some activists even pretending to — or actually — drink the product in protest. The episode resurfaced in September when Congressman José Medeiros mocked supporters who “pray to aliens and drink detergent.”

Images from the two campaigns circulating online and in newspapers clearly illustrate the opposing forces. On one side are gatherings of children holding weapons, people on leashes, women holding whips, missiles, brawls, punches and shouting. On the other are students with painted faces; young people helping the elderly reach the polls; very elderly people dressed in red, proudly displaying their number 13 stickers; jubilant workers; Indigenous people traveling to vote by navigating the vast Amazonian rivers; and buses full of smiling people. On one side, hatred; on the other, if not love, then humanity.

If the internet has increasingly been programmed in recent years to generate and amplify hatred, Bolsonaro supporters, subjected to digital brainwashing, respond in the streets with the same violence that has been normalized online. For this reason, Lula’s Army “general,” Janones, repeatedly instructed people not to respond, not to insult and not to interact with their opponents’ videos. Anger is often more a product of online manipulation than of a person’s true nature. Janones managed to break this trend — at least temporarily. The evidence can be found in the enormous response of mutual aid, the assistance offered to strangers, and the many humorous posts and messages of thanks that appeared after the goal had been achieved. One post reads: “Social media, groups and algorithms: all these elements influence our mental health. Major technology companies promote radicalization, misogyny, homophobia, conspiracy theories and psychosis.”

Political participation is driven by the desire to exert influence over the world in which we live. When politics becomes detached from reality and from people, this alienation inevitably extends to political participation itself. It is in this sense that the importance of the phenomenon triggered by Janones can be acknowledged: despite its contradictions, it succeeded in awakening a desire for political engagement that had seemed dormant. However, while there are reasons to thank Janones for this awakening of new forms of making policy, the mobilization he generated must not be confused with a solution to the problems that have brought us to this point. An increase in the existing delirium cannot be the answer. This dynamic is not so far removed from evangelicalism. Rather than empowering people to exercise self-determination and develop independent thought, it promotes obedience to seemingly unquestionable orders. Political participation must not become a new form of submission, even when it is presented under the banner of a legitimate cause. It is also in this light that Lula’s recent transformation in political communication must be considered. If, until just three weeks ago, there were complaints about the inability to reach the masses online, it is nevertheless questionable that, in such a short time, his channel — created in response to the risk of the Army channel being shut down — has begun publishing daily videos about the day-to-day lives of the president. It is almost as if viewers were watching a kind of 

Big Brother

 at the Planalto Palace.

For the first time in an electoral process marked by the far right, the progressive camp set the course of the debate, and it did so through a common denominator: starting with people who were highly critical of the Lula government’s communication methods, it created a climate of mobilization not seen for decades. 

Mídia Ninja

, an independent journalism and action collective that emerged in the context of the major protests against the PT government and the mobilizations against the World Cup and the Olympics in 2014–6, alongside 342 Artes, a collective mobilizing cultural icons, produced incisive coverage combining memes, news and supportive videos from well-known artists. 

Piauí

 magazine provided extensive coverage of the ties between the businesspeople and bankers who colluded with Bolsonaro, and of the reasons why he might have sought to flee. The 

Revelando

 project, created with the 

Calma Urgente

 podcast team, reconstructed the criminal activities of the Bolsonaro family and their allies in an educational format. Behind these initiatives are professional journalists, fact-checkers and researchers working with 

ICL Notícias

, 

The Intercept Brasil

, 

CartaCapital

 and other outlets. They were joined by the strength of independent Indigenous communications, which allowed information to circulate beyond local networks: A

PIB Oficial, Midiaindigena, Amazonia Coiabamazonia, Apoinme_brasil, Arpinsuloficial, Cons.terena, Yvyrupa.cgy and Sostabajos

, as well as the social-media accounts of Sonia Guajajara and Celia Xakriabá, among many others.

Lula’s intention to make his final presidential term the best of his political journey is evident in the determination with which he has begun, focusing on social initiatives and almost confirming Acemoglu’s suggestion at the beginning of this article. Such a return would also mean revisiting the legacy of Gilberto Gil’s tenure as minister of culture during Lula’s first presidency, which represented one of the most revolutionary steps in integrating digital culture and technological thinking into the Brazilian state, anticipating and shaping crucial debates on copyright, network architecture and data flows. It is time, perhaps, to return to those principles — and to reject the tone of the traditional press.

author: Pierre-Christophe Gam
title: Who gets to dream the future?
content:
We are living in unprecedented times. The world as we know it is changing rapidly as progress in AI and biomedicine is promising to radically transform our lives. We hear talk of humans merging with machines; of the possibility in the near future of uploading our consciousness into the cloud; of editing our DNA to end all diseases and augment our physical abilities; of genetically modified human beings; of human clones and hybrids. We hear talk of lab-grown meat, bio-engineered food and seeds edited to be sterile, rendering us permanently dependent on their patent owners.

We hear talk of a digital grid of control superimposed on our lives; of a future without privacy, without private thoughts or actions, of social credit score systems constantly monitoring and managing behavior; of brain implants recording our thoughts and altering our perception of reality; of the end of government and the rise of AI-controlled city-states run by mega-corporations; and of the collapse of democratic rule in favor of a neo-feudal order shaped by a radical racist, ableist, eugenicist worldview.

All these dystopian scenarios are not merely the science-fiction-informed fantasies of the leading Silicon Valley tycoons. They are also real, circulating scenarios of the future promoted in mainstream media, podcasts, and elite discourse. Since the reelection of Donald Trump and his theatrical inauguration ceremony, surrounded by the owners of the worldʼs largest tech companies, a new ideology has gained ground. Presented as the core philosophy of Silicon Valley elites, the “dark enlightenment” is the name coined for a neo-reactionary project for society.

Think of it as an apocalyptic cult, a quasi-religious project of radical social destruction, committed to the abolition of the democratic values and ideals of inclusive governance and social equity of the post–Second World War era. It envisions a future world structured around rigid, top-down social hierarchies, central authority, and techno-authoritarian control. Peter Thiel, a cofounder of Palantir, is the movement’s best-known backer, and now, with J. D. Vance, his protégé, as vice president, and with Elon Musk, the self-styled transhumanist czar and the largest financial backer of far-right movements across the world, the realization of this vision has never felt more imminent.

Whatʼs perhaps most disturbing beyond the fascist ambitions of this nefarious project is the near silence surrounding it. We are all witnessing the rise of a radical, global movement, a project bent on the total reprogramming of our societies and the destruction of our social norms, and yet it seems as if no one is challenging it, or even acknowledging its presence. But who gave this small circle of socially maladjusted tech nerds the right to decide the collective future of humanity?

The answer is simple. No one.

But who gets to dream the future? Is the future self-arising, an unavoidable destination without possibility for rerouting or adjustment?
